Q30. Why should a process model be tailored?
A. Every model is identical
B. Tailoring removes accountability
C. Projects differ in size, risk, regulation, and uncertainty
D. It makes testing optional
Answer: C. Projects differ in size, risk, regulation, and uncertainty
Why: Tailoring keeps useful controls while avoiding unnecessary process overhead.
Q31. A project must deliver usable features every few weeks. Which approach best supports this?
A. Big-bang development
B. One final release
C. Iterative and incremental development
D. Code-and-fix only
Answer: C. Iterative and incremental development
Why: Incremental releases provide working functionality in stages.
Q32. A prototype is built to clarify uncertain user needs. What is its main purpose?
A. Replace all final testing
B. Explore and validate requirements
C. Guarantee zero defects
D. Freeze the architecture permanently
Answer: B. Explore and validate requirements
Why: A prototype helps stakeholders evaluate and clarify requirements.
Q33. Which model is organized into repeated cycles that assess risks?
A. Spiral
B. Waterfall
C. Big-bang
D. Code-and-fix
Answer: A. Spiral
Why: Risk analysis guides each spiral cycle.
Q34. A team delivers search first and reporting later. This is:
A. Incremental development
B. One-pass development
C. Retirement
D. Reverse engineering
Answer: A. Incremental development
Why: Incremental development delivers functionality in separate parts.
Q35. Which approach is helpful when users are unsure of requirements?
A. Prototyping
B. Ignoring feedback
C. Big-bang only
D. No planning
Answer: A. Prototyping
Why: A prototype helps users clarify expectations by reviewing an example.
Q36. In the V-model, test planning is related to:
A. Development stages
B. Staff salaries
C. Logo design
D. Sales forecasts
Answer: A. Development stages
Why: The V-model pairs development stages with corresponding test levels.
Q37. What is a major benefit of iterative development?
A. Learning and improving in cycles
B. No need for testing
C. No changes are allowed
D. Guaranteed zero cost
Answer: A. Learning and improving in cycles
Why: Each cycle allows evaluation and refinement.
Q38. Which model is usually sequential?
A. Waterfall
B. Spiral
C. Evolutionary prototyping
D. Agile iterations
Answer: A. Waterfall
Why: Waterfall typically proceeds through ordered phases.
Q39. What is a hybrid process model?
A. A combination of practices from multiple models
B. A model with no activities
C. Only a testing plan
D. A model that forbids change
Answer: A. A combination of practices from multiple models
Why: Hybrid models tailor practices to project needs.
Q40. Why should a process model be selected carefully?
A. Projects have different risks and constraints
B. All projects are identical
C. It removes the need for communication
D. It guarantees success
Answer: A. Projects have different risks and constraints
Why: The model should fit the project's context and uncertainty.


3. Agile Software Development
Q1. Which Agile value favors working software over:
A. Comprehensive documentation
B. Customer collaboration
C. Individuals
D. Responding to change
Answer: A. Comprehensive documentation
Why: Agile values documentation, but prioritizes working software.
Q2. In Scrum, who orders the Product Backlog?
A. Developers' manager
B. Scrum Master
C. Customer support
D. Product Owner
Answer: D. Product Owner
Why: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing product value and ordering backlog items.
Q3. What is the main purpose of a Sprint Review?
A. Estimate employee salaries
B. Assign individual blame
C. Inspect the increment with stakeholders
D. Approve source-code formatting
Answer: C. Inspect the increment with stakeholders
Why: The team and stakeholders inspect outcomes and discuss future adaptations.
Q4. What does a retrospective focus on?
A. Accepting the product from customers
B. Releasing a contract
C. Writing every requirement permanently
D. Improving how the team works
Answer: D. Improving how the team works
Why: The retrospective identifies improvements to teamwork and process.
Q5. A user story usually describes:
A. A test environment only
B. A user need and its value
C. A database index only
D. A deployment password
Answer: B. A user need and its value
Why: Stories express functionality from a user's perspective.
Q6. What is a Product Backlog?
A. A staff attendance sheet
B. An ordered list of work for the product
C. A list of closed defects only
D. A final architecture diagram
Answer: B. An ordered list of work for the product
Why: It contains and orders work that may improve the product.
Q7. Which practice gives frequent feedback on code quality?
A. Annual integration
B. Avoiding automated tests
C. Late manual merging only
D. Continuous integration
Answer: D. Continuous integration
Why: Frequent integration exposes conflicts and defects earlier.
Q8. What does a Sprint Backlog contain?
A. All company projects
B. Only rejected features
C. Selected work and a plan to deliver the Sprint Goal
D. Only production incidents
Answer: C. Selected work and a plan to deliver the Sprint Goal
Why: It is the Developers' plan for achieving the Sprint Goal.
Q9. Which statement about Agile is correct?
A. It welcomes changing requirements
B. It forbids planning
C. It removes customer feedback
D. It requires no testing
Answer: A. It welcomes changing requirements
Why: Agile adapts plans as learning and needs change.
Q10. What is the purpose of a Definition of Done?
A. Rank developers
B. Set shared quality criteria for completed work
C. Freeze all future releases
D. Replace acceptance criteria in every case
Answer: B. Set shared quality criteria for completed work
Why: It creates a shared understanding of the quality needed for an increment.
Q11. Who is responsible for managing the Sprint Backlog work?
A. Only end users
B. Only the Product Owner
C. Only external auditors
D. Developers
Answer: D. Developers
Why: Developers plan and adapt the work needed to meet the Sprint Goal.
Q12. What is velocity commonly used for?
A. Calculating code security
B. Measuring individual worth
C. Proving zero defects
D. Forecasting team delivery from past work
Answer: D. Forecasting team delivery from past work
Why: Velocity can support forecasting, but is not a universal productivity score.
Q13. Which is a risk of misusing velocity?
A. Reviewing trends
B. Using it for local forecasting
C. Comparing teams as if their estimates were identical
D. Discussing capacity
Answer: C. Comparing teams as if their estimates were identical
Why: Estimation scales and team contexts differ, so cross-team comparisons mislead.
Q14. What is a burndown chart used to show?
A. Source-code ownership
B. Database normalization
C. Remaining work over time
D. Security permissions
Answer: C. Remaining work over time
Why: It visualizes how much planned work remains during a timebox.
Q15. What does refactoring aim to do?
A. Remove all comments
B. Improve internal structure without changing behavior
C. Skip regression tests
D. Add a visible feature necessarily
Answer: B. Improve internal structure without changing behavior
Why: Refactoring improves design while preserving externally observable behavior.
Q16. Pair programming involves:
A. Two separate teams never communicating
B. A tester replacing a developer
C. Only reviewing after release
D. Two developers working together at one workstation or task
Answer: D. Two developers working together at one workstation or task
Why: One person may drive while the other reviews and thinks ahead, with roles switching.
Q17. What is a key benefit of a small Sprint increment?
A. Earlier feedback on usable functionality
B. No need to prioritize
C. No need for integration
D. No possibility of defects
Answer: A. Earlier feedback on usable functionality
Why: Small increments expose value and problems earlier.
Q18. What does a Scrum Master primarily do?
A. Help the team use Scrum effectively and remove impediments
B. Assign every coding task
C. Own all product requirements
D. Act as the only tester
Answer: A. Help the team use Scrum effectively and remove impediments
Why: The Scrum Master supports Scrum effectiveness and helps address impediments.
Q19. Which is an example of an impediment?
A. A clear acceptance test
B. A prioritized backlog
C. A completed feature
D. A blocked test environment
Answer: D. A blocked test environment
Why: An impediment obstructs progress and should be addressed.
Q20. What should happen when a new high-value feature appears mid-Sprint?
A. Silently add unlimited work
B. Discuss impact and protect the Sprint Goal
C. Ignore all stakeholders forever
D. Delete completed work
Answer: B. Discuss impact and protect the Sprint Goal
Why: Changes should be handled transparently while maintaining focus on the Sprint Goal.
Q21. What is acceptance criteria?
A. A code indentation rule only
B. A list of employee names
C. Conditions a story must satisfy
D. The team's annual budget
Answer: C. Conditions a story must satisfy
Why: Acceptance criteria make expected story behavior testable.
Q22. Which technique helps split a large story?
A. Separate independent user outcomes
B. Increase its ambiguity
C. Remove acceptance criteria
D. Combine unrelated work
Answer: A. Separate independent user outcomes
Why: Smaller vertical slices deliver independently valuable behavior.
Q23. What is technical debt?
A. A customer invoice
B. Future cost created by expedient design or implementation choices
C. An Agile ceremony
D. A performance benchmark
Answer: B. Future cost created by expedient design or implementation choices
Why: Shortcuts may speed delivery now but make future change more costly.
Q24. Why automate regression tests in Agile?
A. To guarantee security
B. To replace product feedback
C. To quickly check that changes did not break existing behavior
D. To eliminate all exploratory testing
Answer: C. To quickly check that changes did not break existing behavior
Why: Automation supports frequent safe changes, though it does not replace all testing.
Q25. What is an Agile increment?
A. A rejected backlog item
B. An untested idea
C. A planning meeting only
D. A usable step toward the product goal
Answer: D. A usable step toward the product goal
Why: An increment adds integrated, usable product value.
Q26. Which meeting is for daily coordination in Scrum?
A. Retrospective
B. Daily Scrum
C. Sprint Review
D. Release audit
Answer: B. Daily Scrum
Why: The Daily Scrum helps Developers inspect progress and adapt their plan.
Q27. What is the best response to a failed Sprint forecast?
A. Learn from it and improve future planning
B. Increase estimates to look better
C. Punish the team automatically
D. Hide the result
Answer: A. Learn from it and improve future planning
Why: Inspecting causes supports better forecasting and continuous improvement.
Q28. What does customer collaboration help prevent?
A. All documentation
B. All changes
C. Building the wrong solution
D. All technical defects automatically
Answer: C. Building the wrong solution
Why: Frequent collaboration helps validate priorities and expectations.
Q29. Which is consistent with Agile quality?
A. Testing only after all features are complete
B. No code review
C. Continuous testing and integration
D. No definition of done
Answer: C. Continuous testing and integration
Why: Quality practices are integrated into ongoing work.
Q30. Agile is best understood as:
A. One mandatory tool
B. A process with no documentation
C. A guarantee of fixed cost
D. A set of values and principles applied through practices
Answer: D. A set of values and principles applied through practices
Why: Agile is broader than any one framework or tool.
Q31. A team receives useful customer feedback after each short release. What should it do next?
A. Freeze all requirements
B. Use the feedback to reprioritize the backlog
C. Avoid changing the plan
D. Restart the project
Answer: B. Use the feedback to reprioritize the backlog
Why: Agile teams adapt priorities using ongoing feedback.
Q32. What is the primary purpose of a sprint retrospective?
A. Assign blame for defects
B. Demonstrate the product to customers
C. Improve the team’s way of working
D. Approve the annual budget
Answer: C. Improve the team’s way of working
Why: The retrospective identifies practical improvements for future iterations.
Q33. In Scrum, what is the Sprint Goal?
A. The purpose the Sprint aims to achieve
B. A list of employee salaries
C. A final contract
D. A coding language
Answer: A. The purpose the Sprint aims to achieve
Why: The Sprint Goal gives the team a shared objective.
Q34. What does continuous integration involve?
A. Frequently integrating code and checking builds
B. Merging only once a year
C. Avoiding automated checks
D. Testing only after release
Answer: A. Frequently integrating code and checking builds
Why: Frequent integration helps reveal conflicts and defects early.
Q35. What should acceptance criteria describe?
A. Conditions a story must meet
B. Team vacation dates
C. Only code formatting
D. The company logo
Answer: A. Conditions a story must meet
Why: Acceptance criteria make expected behavior clear and testable.
Q36. What is the main value of a Sprint Review?
A. Inspecting the increment and gathering feedback
B. Assigning blame
C. Replacing all tests
D. Setting employee salaries
Answer: A. Inspecting the increment and gathering feedback
Why: Stakeholders inspect outcomes and discuss adaptations.
Q37. Why do Agile teams refactor code?
A. Improve structure while preserving behavior
B. Remove all tests
C. Change behavior secretly
D. Avoid design
Answer: A. Improve structure while preserving behavior
Why: Refactoring improves internal design without changing external behavior.
Q38. What is a common use of a burndown chart?
A. Showing remaining work over time
B. Showing user passwords
C. Listing code owners
D. Measuring screen colors
Answer: A. Showing remaining work over time
Why: A burndown chart tracks remaining work during a timebox.
Q39. Who is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog?
A. Product Owner
B. Scrum Master
C. External auditor
D. Every customer individually
Answer: A. Product Owner
Why: The Product Owner orders backlog items to maximize value.
Q40. What should a team do with feedback from a release?
A. Use it to adjust priorities
B. Ignore it permanently
C. Delete the backlog
D. Stop testing
Answer: A. Use it to adjust priorities
Why: Feedback helps the team adapt its product direction.


4. Software Requirements Engineering
Q1. What is requirements elicitation?
A. Measuring CPU usage
B. Deploying the system
C. Discovering needs from stakeholders
D. Writing source code
Answer: C. Discovering needs from stakeholders
Why: Elicitation gathers requirements through interviews, observation, workshops, and other methods.
Q2. Which technique is best for observing real work practices?
A. Version tagging
B. Contextual observation
C. Code compilation
D. Load testing
Answer: B. Contextual observation
Why: Observation can reveal actual workflows and needs users may not mention.
Q3. A requirement says 'the app must be fast.' Its main problem is:
A. Too much precision
B. Too many constraints
C. Excessive traceability
D. Ambiguity and lack of measurability
Answer: D. Ambiguity and lack of measurability
Why: Fast is subjective unless measurable performance targets are specified.
Q4. Which is a functional requirement?
A. Pages load within one second
B. The service has 99.9% availability
C. The system locks an account after five failed logins
D. Data is encrypted at rest
Answer: C. The system locks an account after five failed logins
Why: It describes a specific system behavior.
Q5. Which is a constraint?
A. A user can reset a password
B. An order can be cancelled
C. A report can be exported
D. The product must use the approved database platform
Answer: D. The product must use the approved database platform
Why: A technology mandate restricts design choices.
Q6. What is requirements prioritization used for?
A. Deciding what matters most under constraints
B. Choosing variable names
C. Removing stakeholder input
D. Proving requirements are correct
Answer: A. Deciding what matters most under constraints
Why: Prioritization helps allocate limited time to the highest-value needs.
Q7. What does requirements traceability connect?
A. Only UI colors to logos
B. Requirements to design, code, and tests
C. Only users to passwords
D. Only costs to salaries
Answer: B. Requirements to design, code, and tests
Why: Traceability tracks a requirement through related artifacts and evidence.
Q8. What is a use case mainly used to describe?
A. Actor-system interaction toward a goal
B. Team holiday plan
C. Memory allocation algorithm
D. Code formatting
Answer: A. Actor-system interaction toward a goal
Why: Use cases capture a goal-oriented interaction between actors and the system.
Q9. Who is an actor in a use case?
A. A server CPU
B. A private method
C. A database table
D. An external role interacting with the system
Answer: D. An external role interacting with the system
Why: Actors represent users or external systems that interact with the product.
Q10. What is a requirement baseline?
A. An unreviewed idea list
B. An agreed reference set controlled through change management
C. A test failure report
D. A temporary password
Answer: B. An agreed reference set controlled through change management
Why: A baseline is an approved reference that changes through controlled procedures.
Q11. What is the purpose of a requirements review?
A. Guarantee no future changes
B. Find omissions, conflicts, and ambiguity
C. Replace stakeholder interviews
D. Optimize machine code
Answer: B. Find omissions, conflicts, and ambiguity
Why: Reviews detect problems before requirements guide costly downstream work.
Q12. What is requirements validation?
A. Checking that requirements represent stakeholder needs
B. Measuring team velocity
C. Checking only code syntax
D. Deploying a release
Answer: A. Checking that requirements represent stakeholder needs
Why: Validation confirms the specified requirements describe the right system.
Q13. What does 'shall' often indicate in a formal specification?
A. A completed test
B. A suggestion only
C. An unresolved risk
D. A mandatory requirement
Answer: D. A mandatory requirement
Why: Formal specifications commonly use shall for normative, required behavior.
Q14. Which requirement is most testable?
A. The interface should be attractive
B. 95% of reports finish within 3 seconds for 500 concurrent users
C. The system should be modern
D. The report should be quick
Answer: B. 95% of reports finish within 3 seconds for 500 concurrent users
Why: It gives measurable conditions that can be verified objectively.
Q15. What is a requirements conflict?
A. A test passes
B. A requirement has an ID
C. A user story has an estimate
D. Two requirements cannot both be satisfied as written
Answer: D. Two requirements cannot both be satisfied as written
Why: Conflicting requirements demand resolution with stakeholders.
Q16. What is a domain requirement?
A. A requirement about font size only
B. A requirement arising from the application domain
C. A coding convention
D. A developer's vacation request
Answer: B. A requirement arising from the application domain
Why: Domain knowledge, rules, or regulations may impose specific requirements.
Q17. Why use a glossary?
A. Replace all models
B. Keep domain terms consistent
C. Avoid stakeholder discussion
D. Guarantee performance
Answer: B. Keep domain terms consistent
Why: A shared glossary reduces misunderstandings over terminology.
Q18. What is a business rule?
A. A test runner
B. A policy or constraint governing business behavior
C. A UI animation
D. A source-code comment
Answer: B. A policy or constraint governing business behavior
Why: Business rules express organizational policies or domain logic.
Q19. Which is an example of an interface requirement?
A. The system is easy to learn
B. The team uses two-week Sprints
C. The server has 99% availability
D. The service exchanges JSON through a defined REST endpoint
Answer: D. The service exchanges JSON through a defined REST endpoint
Why: It specifies how the system communicates with another component.
Q20. What is requirements volatility?
A. How frequently requirements change
B. The code's execution speed
C. The number of developers
D. The size of a database
Answer: A. How frequently requirements change
Why: Volatility describes the rate or extent of requirement changes.
Q21. What is a stakeholder interview best suited for?
A. Finding memory leaks directly
B. Measuring throughput
C. Exploring goals, concerns, and constraints
D. Merging branches
Answer: C. Exploring goals, concerns, and constraints
Why: Interviews let analysts probe stakeholder expectations and reasoning.
Q22. Why create a requirements model?
A. Make complex needs easier to analyze and communicate
B. Replace the real system permanently
C. Prevent all change
D. Hide assumptions
Answer: A. Make complex needs easier to analyze and communicate
Why: Models make structure, behavior, and relationships clearer.
Q23. What is an acceptance test derived from?
A. Only server logs
B. Random code style choices
C. Acceptance criteria and agreed requirements
D. Employee attendance
Answer: C. Acceptance criteria and agreed requirements
Why: Acceptance tests check whether agreed user-facing conditions are met.
Q24. What is a non-functional requirement about security?
A. A user can create an appointment
B. A patient can update a phone number
C. Only authorized users can access medical records
D. A clerk can print a receipt
Answer: C. Only authorized users can access medical records
Why: Access control is a security quality constraint.
Q25. What is a common result of missing requirements?
A. Guaranteed faster delivery
B. Lower uncertainty
C. Expensive rework and unmet expectations
D. No defects
Answer: C. Expensive rework and unmet expectations
Why: Missing needs may be discovered late, when changes cost more.
Q26. Which elicitation method gathers ideas from many stakeholders together?
A. Profiling
B. Workshop
C. Unit testing
D. Code review
Answer: B. Workshop
Why: A facilitated workshop helps uncover needs, disagreements, and priorities.
Q27. What is a precondition in a use case?
A. The final test report
B. A code branch
C. A post-release patch
D. A condition that must hold before the interaction starts
Answer: D. A condition that must hold before the interaction starts
Why: Preconditions state assumptions required before the use case begins.
Q28. What is a postcondition?
A. A risk score
B. A state expected after successful completion
C. A stakeholder list
D. A deployment environment
Answer: B. A state expected after successful completion
Why: Postconditions describe the resulting state after the use case.
Q29. What should happen to a proposed requirement change?
A. Assess impact and approve it through the agreed process
B. Apply it without recording
C. Reject all changes automatically
D. Delete the baseline
Answer: A. Assess impact and approve it through the agreed process
Why: Impact analysis and change control reveal effects on scope, cost, design, and tests.
Q30. Which artifact helps prove every requirement has test coverage?
A. Class diagram alone
B. Requirements traceability matrix
C. Burndown chart
D. Risk register
Answer: B. Requirements traceability matrix
Why: A traceability matrix links requirements to corresponding tests and other artifacts.
Q31. Two stakeholders give conflicting rules for the same feature. What is the best next step?
A. Choose the easier rule
B. Implement both without discussion
C. Resolve the conflict with stakeholders
D. Ignore the less senior stakeholder
Answer: C. Resolve the conflict with stakeholders
Why: Conflicting requirements must be negotiated and agreed before implementation.
Q32. Which requirement is most objectively testable?
A. The screen should look modern
B. The system should be easy
C. Search results shall appear within two seconds for 95% of requests
D. The application should feel powerful
Answer: C. Search results shall appear within two seconds for 95% of requests
Why: A measurable threshold makes the requirement verifiable.
Q33. Which technique gathers requirements through group discussion?
A. Workshop
B. Compilation
C. Load testing
D. Branch merging
Answer: A. Workshop
Why: Workshops let stakeholders discuss needs and disagreements together.
Q34. A requirement that says 'easy to use' is weak because it is:
A. Not measurable enough
B. Too specific
C. A source-code error
D. A test result
Answer: A. Not measurable enough
Why: Vague terms should be replaced with observable usability criteria.
Q35. What does a use case describe?
A. An actor's interaction with a system to reach a goal
B. A developer's salary
C. A CPU benchmark
D. A code style rule
Answer: A. An actor's interaction with a system to reach a goal
Why: Use cases describe goal-oriented interactions.
Q36. What is requirements traceability useful for?
A. Following requirements through design and tests
B. Choosing a team name
C. Reducing screen brightness
D. Replacing change control
Answer: A. Following requirements through design and tests
Why: Traceability links requirements to related artifacts and evidence.
Q37. Which is a non-functional requirement?
A. The system shall respond within two seconds
B. A user can create an account
C. A clerk can print a receipt
D. A customer can cancel an order
Answer: A. The system shall respond within two seconds
Why: Response time specifies a performance quality.
Q38. What is requirements volatility?
A. How often requirements change
B. How fast code runs
C. How many users log in
D. How many tests pass
Answer: A. How often requirements change
Why: Volatility describes the frequency or extent of requirement changes.
Q39. What should analysts do when requirements conflict?
A. Resolve the conflict with stakeholders
B. Implement both blindly
C. Ignore one without discussion
D. Delete all requirements
Answer: A. Resolve the conflict with stakeholders
Why: Stakeholders need to agree on a consistent set of needs.
Q40. What is a requirement baseline?
A. An approved set controlled through change management
B. A random idea list
C. A production crash
D. A code editor
Answer: A. An approved set controlled through change management
Why: A baseline is an agreed reference set whose changes are controlled.


5. Software Project Management
Q1. The project scope is expanded without adjusting time or cost. This is:
A. Benchmarking
B. Scope creep
C. Refactoring
D. Validation
Answer: B. Scope creep
Why: Uncontrolled scope growth adds work without matching plan adjustments.
Q2. Which document formally authorizes a project?
A. Code review
B. Test log
C. User manual
D. Project charter
Answer: D. Project charter
Why: A charter establishes the project and gives the project manager authority.
Q3. What does a Gantt chart show?
A. Security threats only
B. Code coverage
C. Activities against calendar time
D. Class inheritance only
Answer: C. Activities against calendar time
Why: A Gantt chart displays tasks, durations, and schedule relationships.
Q4. The critical path is the sequence with:
A. The lowest cost only
B. The most test cases
C. The longest duration determining project finish
D. The most developers
Answer: C. The longest duration determining project finish
Why: A delay on the critical path generally delays the project completion date.
Q5. What is a project milestone?
A. A daily coding instruction
B. A significant checkpoint or event
C. A database field
D. A software defect
Answer: B. A significant checkpoint or event
Why: Milestones mark important events and are often zero-duration schedule points.
Q6. A task slips but has float available. The finish date may:
A. Automatically reduce scope
B. Become impossible to estimate
C. Remain unchanged if the float absorbs the delay
D. Always move by the same amount
Answer: C. Remain unchanged if the float absorbs the delay
Why: Float is schedule flexibility before a dependent date is affected.
Q7. What is effort estimation usually measured in?
A. Screen colors
B. Person-hours or person-months
C. Defect names
D. Number of meetings only
Answer: B. Person-hours or person-months
Why: Effort estimates represent labor, distinct from elapsed calendar duration.
Q8. Why can adding people to a late project make it later?
A. Tasks become independent automatically
B. Coordination and onboarding add overhead
C. More people always reduce communication
D. Testing is removed
Answer: B. Coordination and onboarding add overhead
Why: New staff need context and create communication overhead; not all work is parallelizable.
Q9. What is a risk register used for?
A. Recording risks, owners, responses, and status
B. Listing completed invoices
C. Storing source code only
D. Tracking UI colors
Answer: A. Recording risks, owners, responses, and status
Why: A risk register supports active monitoring and response planning.
Q10. What is earned value management used to compare?
A. Only code lines
B. Only team attendance
C. Planned value, earned value, and actual cost
D. Only user satisfaction
Answer: C. Planned value, earned value, and actual cost
Why: EVM integrates scope, schedule, and cost performance.
Q11. A project has many dependencies. What should the manager maintain?
A. Only a logo
B. A dependency-aware schedule
C. No milestones
D. Only a team chat
Answer: B. A dependency-aware schedule
Why: Dependencies determine task order and influence schedule risk.
Q12. What is a stakeholder communication plan?
A. Guarantees agreement
B. Lists only programming languages
C. Defines who needs what information and when
D. Replaces project status
Answer: C. Defines who needs what information and when
Why: Planned communication keeps relevant people informed at suitable intervals.
Q13. What is resource leveling?
A. Removing all deadlines
B. Adjusting schedules to address resource limits
C. Counting test cases
D. Changing requirements silently
Answer: B. Adjusting schedules to address resource limits
Why: Resource leveling resolves over-allocation by moving work where possible.
Q14. A project has a fixed deadline and variable features. The best control is to:
A. Add every request
B. Stop monitoring
C. Ignore quality
D. Prioritize scope and protect essential outcomes
Answer: D. Prioritize scope and protect essential outcomes
Why: With fixed time, prioritizing scope helps preserve critical value and quality.
Q15. What is a project baseline?
A. An informal guess never approved
B. Approved plan used to compare actual performance
C. A coding standard only
D. A customer complaint
Answer: B. Approved plan used to compare actual performance
Why: Baselines provide reference points for monitoring changes and performance.
Q16. Which is a leading indicator of schedule trouble?
A. Key dependency tasks repeatedly slipping
B. A signed-off feature
C. Final delivery already completed
D. A passing unit test
Answer: A. Key dependency tasks repeatedly slipping
Why: Repeated early slippage signals possible downstream delays.
Q17. What is a change request?
A. A random chat message only
B. A defect-free build
C. A staff appraisal
D. A formal proposal to alter an approved project element
Answer: D. A formal proposal to alter an approved project element
Why: A change request allows impacts to be assessed and a decision recorded.
Q18. What does project governance provide?
A. Only code execution
B. Decision rights, oversight, and accountability
C. Only source formatting
D. Automatic risk elimination
Answer: B. Decision rights, oversight, and accountability
Why: Governance clarifies who decides, monitors, and is accountable.
Q19. What is a project assumption?
A. A planning belief treated as true until verified
B. A signed contract clause always
C. A closed defect
D. A confirmed test result
Answer: A. A planning belief treated as true until verified
Why: Assumptions affect plans and should be tracked because they may prove false.
Q20. Why should project status be evidence-based?
A. It makes bad news disappear
B. It replaces estimates
C. It guarantees no delay
D. It supports realistic decisions and corrective action
Answer: D. It supports realistic decisions and corrective action
Why: Reliable data exposes deviations early and supports sound action.
Q21. Which metric indicates schedule performance in EVM?
A. SPI = EV / PV
B. Defects / KLOC
C. CPI = AC / EV
D. Passes / failures
Answer: A. SPI = EV / PV
Why: Schedule Performance Index compares earned value with planned value.
Q22. Which metric indicates cost performance in EVM?
A. CPI = EV / AC
B. Risk / feature
C. SPI = EV / PV
D. Lines / developer
Answer: A. CPI = EV / AC
Why: Cost Performance Index compares earned value with actual cost.
Q23. What is a project constraint?
A. A new feature idea only
B. A code comment
C. A passing test
D. A limit such as budget, time, or resources
Answer: D. A limit such as budget, time, or resources
Why: Constraints bound the options available to the project.
Q24. What is the purpose of a lessons-learned review?
A. Erase project records
B. Capture practices to improve future work
C. Assign blame only
D. Replace acceptance testing
Answer: B. Capture practices to improve future work
Why: Lessons learned turn experience into reusable organizational knowledge.
Q25. A vendor misses a delivery date. What should the manager first consult?
A. Only source indentation
B. No documentation
C. Contract, dependency impact, and contingency plan
D. Only UI mock-ups
Answer: C. Contract, dependency impact, and contingency plan
Why: The response depends on commitments, impact, and available alternatives.
Q26. What is a work breakdown structure?
A. A security algorithm
B. A hierarchical decomposition of project deliverables and work
C. A release binary
D. A user survey
Answer: B. A hierarchical decomposition of project deliverables and work
Why: The WBS breaks project scope into manageable components.
Q27. Why define acceptance criteria early?
A. To make completion and acceptance measurable
B. To avoid testing
C. To remove scope
D. To prevent user feedback
Answer: A. To make completion and acceptance measurable
Why: Agreed criteria reduce disputes about whether a deliverable is complete.
Q28. What is the purpose of a project buffer?
A. Protect a schedule against uncertainty
B. Replace all estimates
C. Remove dependencies
D. Increase scope without approval
Answer: A. Protect a schedule against uncertainty
Why: A buffer provides planned contingency for uncertainty.
Q29. What is resource over-allocation?
A. Finishing early
B. Using version control
C. Assigning more work than a resource can reasonably perform
D. Having no tasks
Answer: C. Assigning more work than a resource can reasonably perform
Why: Over-allocation creates competing demands and likely delays.
Q30. What is the manager's best response to a major deviation?
A. Ignore stakeholder needs
B. Analyze cause, impact, and corrective options
C. Hide it until release
D. Change the baseline without approval
Answer: B. Analyze cause, impact, and corrective options
Why: Corrective action should follow evidence and approved change control.
Q31. A task on the critical path is delayed by three days. What is the likely effect if nothing changes?
A. The project finish may be delayed by three days
B. No task can be affected
C. The budget automatically decreases
D. The scope is reduced automatically
Answer: A. The project finish may be delayed by three days
Why: A critical-path delay generally delays the project end date unless recovered.
Q32. What does a work breakdown structure organize?
A. Project work into manageable parts
B. Only source code lines
C. User passwords
D. Test colors
Answer: A. Project work into manageable parts
Why: A WBS decomposes scope into manageable deliverables and work.
Q33. Which chart displays tasks against calendar time?
A. Gantt chart
B. Class diagram
C. State diagram
D. Use-case diagram
Answer: A. Gantt chart
Why: A Gantt chart shows activities, durations, and schedule.
Q34. What does a project milestone represent?
A. An important checkpoint or event
B. A line of code
C. A defect type
D. A user password
Answer: A. An important checkpoint or event
Why: Milestones mark significant project events.
Q35. What is scope creep?
A. Uncontrolled growth in project scope
B. A planned code review
C. A test strategy
D. A risk response
Answer: A. Uncontrolled growth in project scope
Why: Scope creep adds work without appropriate control of time, cost, or resources.
Q36. What is the critical path?
A. The longest dependent path that determines finish time
B. The cheapest task
C. The list of optional features
D. The test team's roster
Answer: A. The longest dependent path that determines finish time
Why: Delays on the critical path can delay project completion.
Q37. Why maintain a risk register?
A. Track risks, owners, responses, and status
B. Store source code only
C. Replace the schedule
D. Record UI colors
Answer: A. Track risks, owners, responses, and status
Why: A risk register supports monitoring and response planning.
Q38. What is effort commonly measured in?
A. Person-hours or person-months
B. Screen sizes
C. Defect labels
D. Calendar names
Answer: A. Person-hours or person-months
Why: Effort measures labor, while duration measures elapsed time.
Q39. What should a manager do when a major deviation appears?
A. Analyze causes, impact, and corrective actions
B. Hide the information
C. Change the baseline secretly
D. Ignore the team
Answer: A. Analyze causes, impact, and corrective actions
Why: Evidence-based analysis supports appropriate corrective action.
Q40. Which practice helps keep project scope under control?
A. Formal change control
B. Silent feature additions
C. Skipping estimates
D. Removing milestones
Answer: A. Formal change control
Why: Change control assesses the impact and approval of proposed scope changes.


6. Software Design
Q1. Which design principle gives a module one focused responsibility?
A. High coupling
B. Duplication
C. High cohesion
D. Global state
Answer: C. High cohesion
Why: High cohesion means a module's elements support a closely related purpose.
Q2. Why is low coupling desirable?
A. Testing becomes impossible
B. Every module shares all data
C. The system has no interfaces
D. Modules can change with fewer ripple effects
Answer: D. Modules can change with fewer ripple effects
Why: Low coupling limits dependencies between modules.
Q3. Which is a sign of poor modular design?
A. Focused responsibilities
B. Clear module interfaces
C. Independent unit tests
D. A small change requires edits across many modules
Answer: D. A small change requires edits across many modules
Why: Widespread edits suggest tight coupling or weak boundaries.
Q4. What does abstraction do?
A. Prevents reuse
B. Removes all interfaces
C. Adds every implementation detail
D. Hides irrelevant detail behind essential concepts
Answer: D. Hides irrelevant detail behind essential concepts
Why: Abstraction lets designers reason about important behavior without unnecessary detail.
Q5. What does encapsulation protect?
A. Only user documentation
B. The schedule
C. Internal state behind a defined interface
D. Every variable globally
Answer: C. Internal state behind a defined interface
Why: Encapsulation controls access to implementation details and invariants.
Q6. Which UML diagram best shows object interactions over time?
A. Sequence diagram
B. Deployment diagram
C. State-independent glossary
D. Package diagram
Answer: A. Sequence diagram
Why: Sequence diagrams show messages between participants in time order.
Q7. Which UML diagram models states and transitions?
A. Component diagram
B. Use-case list
C. State machine diagram
D. Class diagram
Answer: C. State machine diagram
Why: State machines model behavior triggered by events and guarded transitions.
Q8. What does a class diagram primarily represent?
A. Test execution time
B. Project cost
C. Network hardware placement only
D. Classes, attributes, operations, and relationships
Answer: D. Classes, attributes, operations, and relationships
Why: Class diagrams capture static structural relationships.
Q9. A subclass can replace its parent without breaking expected behavior. This supports:
A. Waterfall principle
B. Open database principle
C. Least privilege
D. Liskov substitution principle
Answer: D. Liskov substitution principle
Why: Subtypes should honor the behavioral expectations of their base types.
Q10. Which principle recommends one reason for a class to change?
A. Dependency Inversion Principle
B. Interface Segregation Principle
C. Single Responsibility Principle
D. Open/Closed Principle
Answer: C. Single Responsibility Principle
Why: A class should have one focused responsibility and reason to change.
Q11. The Open/Closed Principle says modules should be:
A. Open to extension, closed to modification
B. Open to all data
C. Closed to testing
D. Closed to reuse
Answer: A. Open to extension, closed to modification
Why: New behavior should often be added through extension rather than repeated edits to stable code.
Q12. Dependency inversion favors depending on:
A. Global variables
B. User interface colors
C. Specific database tables everywhere
D. Abstractions rather than concrete details
Answer: D. Abstractions rather than concrete details
Why: Abstractions reduce direct dependencies on implementation details.
Q13. Which pattern lets an object notify subscribers when its state changes?
A. Factory Method
B. Singleton
C. Observer
D. Adapter
Answer: C. Observer
Why: Observer defines a one-to-many notification relationship.
Q14. Which pattern creates objects without exposing the exact creation logic to callers?
A. Factory Method
B. Decorator
C. Observer
D. State
Answer: A. Factory Method
Why: Factory Method delegates object creation to a method that subclasses can specialize.
Q15. Which pattern wraps an object to add behavior dynamically?
A. Iterator
B. Decorator
C. Command
D. Observer
Answer: B. Decorator
Why: Decorator adds responsibilities through a compatible wrapper.
Q16. Which pattern converts one interface into another expected by a client?
A. Builder
B. Adapter
C. Singleton
D. Observer
Answer: B. Adapter
Why: Adapter translates a class interface to the one clients expect.
Q17. Why prefer composition over inheritance in many designs?
A. It guarantees zero coupling
B. It prevents reuse
C. It removes object behavior
D. It can reduce rigid class hierarchies
Answer: D. It can reduce rigid class hierarchies
Why: Composition builds behavior from collaborators and can be more flexible than deep inheritance.
Q18. What is design by contract concerned with?
A. Only code indentation
B. Only deployment regions
C. Preconditions, postconditions, and invariants
D. Only story points
Answer: C. Preconditions, postconditions, and invariants
Why: Contracts specify obligations before and guarantees after operations.
Q19. What is a design invariant?
A. A user story estimate
B. A condition that must remain true
C. A temporary log message
D. A random input
Answer: B. A condition that must remain true
Why: Invariants preserve consistency across operations and states.
Q20. Which design is easier to unit test?
A. One with tangled responsibilities
B. One with clear interfaces and limited dependencies
C. One requiring the whole system for every test
D. One with hidden global state everywhere
Answer: B. One with clear interfaces and limited dependencies
Why: Isolation and clear boundaries make behavior easier to test.
Q21. What is a design smell?
A. A security certificate
B. A warning sign of a possible design problem
C. A proof of a runtime failure
D. A project milestone
Answer: B. A warning sign of a possible design problem
Why: Smells suggest code may need closer review or refactoring.
Q22. Why avoid duplicated business rules?
A. They can drift and produce inconsistent behavior
B. They improve traceability automatically
C. They remove coupling
D. They always run faster
Answer: A. They can drift and produce inconsistent behavior
Why: Copies may be updated differently, causing inconsistent outcomes.
Q23. What is an interface in object-oriented design?
A. A contract of available operations
B. A test failure
C. A database backup
D. A release schedule
Answer: A. A contract of available operations
Why: Interfaces define what clients can call without prescribing all implementation details.
Q24. Which design choice helps localize change?
A. Exposing internal fields
B. Duplicating algorithms
C. Sharing mutable globals
D. Encapsulating volatile details
Answer: D. Encapsulating volatile details
Why: Encapsulation isolates likely-to-change decisions behind stable boundaries.
Q25. What is a sequence diagram lifeline?
A. A participant's existence during an interaction
B. A test suite
C. A class's memory size
D. A network firewall
Answer: A. A participant's existence during an interaction
Why: A lifeline represents a participant over the interaction timeline.
Q26. What does a dependency arrow commonly indicate in a UML class diagram?
A. A user logs in
B. A test passed
C. A release was deployed
D. One element relies on another
Answer: D. One element relies on another
Why: A dependency shows that changes to a supplier may affect its client.
Q27. Which is the best reason to use a design pattern?
A. Guarantee perfect performance
B. Add complexity to every class
C. Apply a known solution when the context fits
D. Avoid understanding requirements
Answer: C. Apply a known solution when the context fits
Why: Patterns provide reusable design ideas, but must suit the actual problem.
Q28. What is cohesion measured qualitatively by?
A. How many releases exist
B. How strongly a module's elements belong together
C. How many unrelated modules it calls
D. How many users it has
Answer: B. How strongly a module's elements belong together
Why: A cohesive module focuses on a unified responsibility.
Q29. Which design is most extensible?
A. Editing many unrelated modules for each payment
B. Using hard-coded type checks everywhere
C. Adding a new payment type through a stable abstraction
D. Duplicating payment logic
Answer: C. Adding a new payment type through a stable abstraction
Why: Stable abstractions allow new implementations with fewer changes to existing code.
Q30. Why should design be reviewed before implementation?
A. To avoid stakeholder feedback
B. To replace all testing
C. To guarantee no requirements change
D. To catch structural problems before they become costly
Answer: D. To catch structural problems before they become costly
Why: Early review can uncover expensive architectural and modular mistakes.
Q31. A module exposes only the operations other modules need. Which principle is being applied?
A. High coupling
B. Information hiding
C. Duplicate logic
D. Global state
Answer: B. Information hiding
Why: Information hiding conceals internal details behind a clear interface.
Q32. Which design principle keeps a module focused on one purpose?
A. High cohesion
B. High coupling
C. Global state
D. Duplication
Answer: A. High cohesion
Why: High cohesion means a module's elements serve a closely related purpose.
Q33. What does abstraction help a designer do?
A. Focus on essential details
B. Expose every internal detail
C. Remove all interfaces
D. Prevent reuse
Answer: A. Focus on essential details
Why: Abstraction hides irrelevant complexity.
Q34. Which design choice usually reduces ripple effects?
A. Low coupling
B. Shared global state
C. Duplicated logic
D. Large monolithic modules
Answer: A. Low coupling
Why: Low coupling limits dependencies between modules.
Q35. What does encapsulation place behind a defined interface?
A. Internal state and implementation details
B. The project budget
C. The release calendar
D. User training
Answer: A. Internal state and implementation details
Why: Encapsulation controls access to internal state.
Q36. Which UML diagram shows messages in time order?
A. Sequence diagram
B. Deployment diagram
C. Package diagram
D. Class glossary
Answer: A. Sequence diagram
Why: Sequence diagrams show interactions over time.
Q37. What does a class diagram mainly show?
A. Classes and their relationships
B. Calendar tasks
C. Network traffic only
D. Test execution time
Answer: A. Classes and their relationships
Why: Class diagrams represent static structure.
Q38. Why use design patterns?
A. Reuse proven solutions to recurring design problems
B. Guarantee no defects
C. Replace requirements
D. Avoid all documentation
Answer: A. Reuse proven solutions to recurring design problems
Why: Patterns describe reusable approaches to common design problems.
Q39. What is a design interface?
A. A defined way components interact
B. A staff attendance sheet
C. A budget report
D. A production incident
Answer: A. A defined way components interact
Why: Interfaces specify how components communicate.
Q40. Which design quality helps a component be tested independently?
A. Low coupling
B. Global state
C. Duplicated logic
D. Hidden dependencies
Answer: A. Low coupling
Why: Low coupling reduces reliance on other components.


7. Software Architecture
Q1. Software architecture mainly describes:
A. Every variable name
B. Only screen colors
C. Major components and their relationships
D. Only project invoices
Answer: C. Major components and their relationships
Why: Architecture captures the system's high-level structure and important decisions.
Q2. Which style separates presentation, business logic, and data access?
A. Event log only
B. Layered architecture
C. Peer-to-peer only
D. Pipe-free monolith
Answer: B. Layered architecture
Why: Layering separates responsibilities into tiers with defined dependencies.
Q3. What is a key advantage of a microservices architecture?
A. It removes network failures
B. All services share one release always
C. Services can often be deployed independently
D. It requires no monitoring
Answer: C. Services can often be deployed independently
Why: Independent services can evolve separately, though operations become more complex.
Q4. What is a common microservices challenge?
A. No need for data management
B. No independent deployment possible
C. No service boundaries
D. Distributed communication and operations
Answer: D. Distributed communication and operations
Why: Network calls, observability, and data consistency introduce complexity.
Q5. Which architecture style connects processing steps through data streams?
A. Blackboard only
B. Repository only
C. Pipe-and-filter
D. Layered
Answer: C. Pipe-and-filter
Why: Filters transform data and pipes carry it between stages.
Q6. In a client-server system, the server typically:
A. Provides services requested by clients
B. Cannot serve multiple clients
C. Only stores client screen colors
D. Must run on every user's device
Answer: A. Provides services requested by clients
Why: Servers expose services or resources to clients over a network.
Q7. What is a repository architecture centered on?
A. A shared data store accessed by components
B. A project budget
C. A sequence of filters only
D. A single user interface widget
Answer: A. A shared data store accessed by components
Why: Components communicate through a central shared data repository.
Q8. What is an architectural quality attribute?
A. Button label
B. Meeting date
C. Availability
D. Variable name
Answer: C. Availability
Why: Availability is a system-wide quality concern that influences architectural choices.
Q9. Why use an architecture decision record?
A. Document a significant decision and its rationale
B. Guarantee the decision never changes
C. Replace source control
D. Record every keystroke
Answer: A. Document a significant decision and its rationale
Why: ADRs preserve the context, alternatives, and reasoning behind key choices.
Q10. What is a system bottleneck?
A. A component limiting overall throughput or response
B. A completed requirement
C. A test fixture
D. A coding comment
Answer: A. A component limiting overall throughput or response
Why: The bottleneck constrains end-to-end performance.
Q11. What does horizontal scaling do?
A. Reduces all traffic to zero
B. Deletes services
C. Adds more instances or machines
D. Only increases one machine's RAM
Answer: C. Adds more instances or machines
Why: Horizontal scaling distributes load across additional instances.
Q12. What does vertical scaling do?
A. Splits a UI into tabs
B. Changes a class name
C. Adds independent service instances only
D. Increases resources of a single machine
Answer: D. Increases resources of a single machine
Why: Vertical scaling increases capacity within one machine.
Q13. What is redundancy used for in architecture?
A. Avoiding backups
B. Making a single point of failure stronger
C. Maintaining service despite component failure
D. Reducing all availability
Answer: C. Maintaining service despite component failure
Why: Redundant components can preserve service when one fails.
Q14. What is a single point of failure?
A. A load-balanced cluster
B. One component whose failure can stop the system
C. A passing test
D. A duplicated backup
Answer: B. One component whose failure can stop the system
Why: If no alternative exists, failure of that component can disrupt the whole service.
Q15. Which style best fits asynchronous event-driven communication?
A. Publish-subscribe
B. Class inheritance
C. Strict single call chain only
D. Waterfall
Answer: A. Publish-subscribe
Why: Publishers emit events and subscribers receive relevant notifications.
Q16. What is eventual consistency?
A. Every read is always globally synchronized
B. No data is replicated
C. All writes are rejected
D. Replicas may temporarily differ but converge if updates stop
Answer: D. Replicas may temporarily differ but converge if updates stop
Why: Distributed replicas may become consistent after propagation delay.
Q17. What is a trade-off in architecture?
A. Testing replaces design
B. Improving one quality may weaken another
C. Every quality improves automatically
D. No decision has consequences
Answer: B. Improving one quality may weaken another
Why: For example, stronger consistency can increase latency or reduce availability.
Q18. Which architecture supports independent UI and service evolution through an API?
A. No-interface architecture
B. Hard-coded screen-to-database access
C. Client-server with a defined API
D. One shared global UI state
Answer: C. Client-server with a defined API
Why: A stable API decouples clients from service implementation.
Q19. What is a deployment diagram used to show?
A. Software artifacts and their runtime nodes
B. User interview notes
C. Class methods only
D. Requirements priorities
Answer: A. Software artifacts and their runtime nodes
Why: Deployment diagrams map software to hardware or execution environments.
Q20. What is an architectural prototype useful for?
A. Replacing the product indefinitely
B. Proving every feature complete
C. Avoiding performance measurement
D. Testing a risky technical assumption early
Answer: D. Testing a risky technical assumption early
Why: A focused prototype tests uncertainty before large investment.
Q21. Why is observability important in distributed systems?
A. It helps infer internal state from logs, metrics, and traces
B. It removes network latency
C. It replaces security
D. It prevents all bugs
Answer: A. It helps infer internal state from logs, metrics, and traces
Why: Observability helps diagnose failures across service boundaries.
Q22. What does fault tolerance mean?
A. The system is always offline
B. The system never experiences faults
C. The system continues providing acceptable service despite some faults
D. The system has no tests
Answer: C. The system continues providing acceptable service despite some faults
Why: Fault-tolerant design anticipates failures and limits their impact.
Q23. Which is a benefit of a monolithic architecture?
A. Every module deploys independently by default
B. Network boundaries are mandatory
C. Data consistency is impossible
D. Simpler deployment and in-process calls for many small systems
Answer: D. Simpler deployment and in-process calls for many small systems
Why: A monolith can be simpler to develop and operate when boundaries and scale permit.
Q24. What is a service boundary intended to do?
A. Remove all ownership
B. Merge unrelated domains
C. Expose every internal database table
D. Define responsibility and interaction contracts
Answer: D. Define responsibility and interaction contracts
Why: Clear boundaries reduce accidental coupling and clarify responsibilities.
Q25. Which concern most strongly affects architecture early?
A. Final typo list
B. Exact variable names
C. Developer desk layout
D. Quality attributes and constraints
Answer: D. Quality attributes and constraints
Why: Performance, security, availability, and constraints shape major structural choices.
Q26. What is load balancing used for?
A. Removing all replicas
B. Distributing requests across available instances
C. Encrypting source code
D. Writing requirements
Answer: B. Distributing requests across available instances
Why: Load balancing spreads traffic and can improve capacity and availability.
Q27. Why should architecture be evaluated with scenarios?
A. Scenarios guarantee no changes
B. Scenarios replace implementation
C. Scenarios are only for UI color
D. Scenarios reveal whether the design meets quality goals
Answer: D. Scenarios reveal whether the design meets quality goals
Why: Concrete scenarios expose architectural strengths, weaknesses, and trade-offs.
Q28. What is technical debt at architecture level?
A. A project loan only
B. Short-term structural shortcuts that raise future change costs
C. A test report
D. A user password
Answer: B. Short-term structural shortcuts that raise future change costs
Why: Architectural shortcuts can make later scaling, change, or reliability harder.
Q29. Which choice can reduce coupling between services?
A. Well-defined APIs and owned data boundaries
B. Shared mutable internal state
C. Directly editing another service's database
D. Circular synchronous calls
Answer: A. Well-defined APIs and owned data boundaries
Why: Explicit contracts and data ownership reduce hidden dependencies.
Q30. Why is architecture not simply a diagram?
A. It only lists source files
B. It excludes quality attributes
C. It includes decisions, constraints, and rationale
D. A diagram is always useless
Answer: C. It includes decisions, constraints, and rationale
Why: Architecture is the set of important structures and decisions, not just a picture.
Q31. A system must let one service change without rebuilding all others. Which architectural concern matters most?
A. Tight coupling
B. Shared global state
C. Service independence
D. Single large executable
Answer: C. Service independence
Why: Independent services reduce the impact of changes across the system.
Q32. What does software architecture describe?
A. Major components and their relationships
B. Only variable names
C. Only screen colors
D. The team's holidays
Answer: A. Major components and their relationships
Why: Architecture captures high-level structure and interactions.
Q33. Which architecture style separates presentation, logic, and data?
A. Layered architecture
B. Big-bang coding
C. Flat file only
D. No architecture
Answer: A. Layered architecture
Why: Layering separates responsibilities into levels.
Q34. What is a benefit of client-server architecture?
A. Responsibilities can be divided between clients and servers
B. It removes all networks
C. It guarantees no downtime
D. It prevents scaling
Answer: A. Responsibilities can be divided between clients and servers
Why: Clients request services and servers provide them.
Q35. What is a microservice typically designed around?
A. A focused business capability
B. One global variable
C. One screen color
D. A project milestone
Answer: A. A focused business capability
Why: Microservices are small, independently deployable services around capabilities.
Q36. What is an architectural trade-off?
A. A benefit in one quality may cost another
B. A guaranteed improvement in every quality
C. A code typo
D. A user interview
Answer: A. A benefit in one quality may cost another
Why: Architecture decisions often balance competing quality attributes.
Q37. Which concern is important in distributed architecture?
A. Network failures and communication delays
B. Only font choice
C. Only variable spelling
D. No interfaces
Answer: A. Network failures and communication delays
Why: Distributed components communicate over networks that can fail or be slow.
Q38. What does scalability mean for architecture?
A. Handling increased workload acceptably
B. Changing a variable name
C. Reducing all features
D. Avoiding monitoring
Answer: A. Handling increased workload acceptably
Why: Scalability is the ability to handle growth in load.
Q39. Why document architectural decisions?
A. Explain rationale and consequences
B. Guarantee the project has no risks
C. Replace implementation
D. Hide trade-offs
Answer: A. Explain rationale and consequences
Why: Decision records help teams understand choices and their impacts.
Q40. Which architecture quality is concerned with protecting data and services?
A. Security
B. Font size
C. Naming style
D. Meeting length
Answer: A. Security
Why: Security decisions protect system assets and control access.


8. User Interface Design
Q1. Which design principle helps users recognize rather than memorize commands?
A. Hidden controls
B. More memory burden
C. Inconsistent labels
D. Recognition over recall
Answer: D. Recognition over recall
Why: Visible options reduce the amount users must remember.
Q2. A destructive action has no confirmation or undo. Which issue is most evident?
A. Good feedback
B. Strong encapsulation
C. Poor error prevention and recovery
D. High portability
Answer: C. Poor error prevention and recovery
Why: Safeguards help prevent costly mistakes and recover from them.
Q3. What does consistency in UI design provide?
A. More user confusion
B. Less learnability
C. Predictable behavior across screens
D. Different controls for identical actions
Answer: C. Predictable behavior across screens
Why: Consistent patterns let users transfer learning from one screen to another.
Q4. Why show feedback after saving a form?
A. Make users guess
B. Replace validation
C. Hide system status
D. Confirm the system received and processed the action
Answer: D. Confirm the system received and processed the action
Why: Feedback communicates the result and current state.
Q5. Which is the best label for a button that submits an order?
A. Do the thing
B. Submit order
C. Continue
D. Click here maybe
Answer: B. Submit order
Why: Specific labels communicate the action and reduce ambiguity.
Q6. What is affordance in interface design?
A. A database backup
B. A network protocol
C. A testing metric
D. A clue about how an element can be used
Answer: D. A clue about how an element can be used
Why: Affordances suggest possible actions, such as a handle suggesting pulling.
Q7. What does accessibility aim to ensure?
A. Only expert users can use it
B. Keyboard use is blocked
C. People with diverse abilities can use the interface
D. Colors carry all information
Answer: C. People with diverse abilities can use the interface
Why: Accessible design supports users with visual, motor, auditory, and cognitive differences.
Q8. Why should color not be the only error indicator?
A. It prevents screen readers
B. Color always slows systems
C. Some users may not distinguish the colors
D. It makes text searchable
Answer: C. Some users may not distinguish the colors
Why: Pair color with text, icons, or patterns so meaning remains available.
Q9. What is usability testing?
A. Asking only developers whether they like it
B. Observing representative users completing tasks
C. Checking compiler errors
D. Measuring server uptime only
Answer: B. Observing representative users completing tasks
Why: Usability tests reveal where users struggle with real tasks.
Q10. Which metric can indicate task usability?
A. Number of developers
B. CPU model name
C. Number of source files
D. Task completion rate
Answer: D. Task completion rate
Why: Completion rate measures whether users successfully finish intended tasks.
Q11. A form rejects an entry but says only 'Error.' What is missing?
A. Source control
B. A new architecture
C. More ambiguity
D. Actionable error guidance
Answer: D. Actionable error guidance
Why: Useful messages explain the problem and how to correct it.
Q12. Why group related form fields?
A. Make navigation random
B. Increase visual noise
C. Hide relationships
D. Reduce cognitive load and clarify structure
Answer: D. Reduce cognitive load and clarify structure
Why: Grouping helps users understand related information and complete tasks.
Q13. What is responsive design?
A. Adapting layout to different screen sizes
B. Making every page identical in size
C. Removing mobile support
D. Using only fixed-width layouts
Answer: A. Adapting layout to different screen sizes
Why: Responsive layouts adjust to viewport and device constraints.
Q14. What is a wireframe?
A. A low-detail layout showing structure and content placement
B. A security token
C. A production server
D. A final database schema
Answer: A. A low-detail layout showing structure and content placement
Why: Wireframes communicate layout before detailed visual styling.
Q15. Why keep navigation labels familiar?
A. It prevents accessibility
B. It makes the site harder to learn
C. Users can predict where links lead
D. It hides page purpose
Answer: C. Users can predict where links lead
Why: Familiar terminology lowers the effort needed to navigate.
Q16. What is a modal dialog best used for?
A. Replacing all navigation
B. Showing unlimited unrelated content
C. Every minor notification
D. A focused task that needs attention before returning
Answer: D. A focused task that needs attention before returning
Why: Modals interrupt the current flow and should be reserved for focused interactions.
Q17. Which is a useful mobile touch target practice?
A. Make controls large and well spaced
B. Hide primary actions
C. Require precise hover
D. Place tiny controls together
Answer: A. Make controls large and well spaced
Why: Larger, spaced targets reduce accidental taps.
Q18. What is information architecture?
A. Estimating project cost
B. Selecting CPU architecture
C. Organizing content and navigation so users can find things
D. Writing unit tests
Answer: C. Organizing content and navigation so users can find things
Why: It structures information, labels, and pathways for findability.
Q19. Why provide undo for reversible actions?
A. It supports recovery from mistakes
B. It removes the need for feedback
C. It prevents all errors
D. It makes tasks irreversible
Answer: A. It supports recovery from mistakes
Why: Undo lowers the cost of accidental actions.
Q20. Which contrast issue can harm readability?
A. Consistent spacing
B. Descriptive labels
C. Clear headings
D. Low text-to-background contrast
Answer: D. Low text-to-background contrast
Why: Sufficient contrast helps people distinguish text from its background.
Q21. What is a persona in UX work?
A. A real user's password
B. A research-based representation of a user group
C. A code module
D. A project milestone
Answer: B. A research-based representation of a user group
Why: Personas summarize goals, needs, and behavior patterns grounded in research.
Q22. What does a user journey map show?
A. Only database fields
B. Only source-code dependencies
C. Steps and experiences across a task or service
D. Only test coverage
Answer: C. Steps and experiences across a task or service
Why: Journey maps reveal touchpoints, pain points, and opportunities.
Q23. Why avoid relying on hover for essential actions?
A. It guarantees discoverability
B. Touch devices may not have hover
C. Hover is required on phones
D. Hover always improves accessibility
Answer: B. Touch devices may not have hover
Why: Touch users need controls that work without hover.
Q24. What is progressive disclosure?
A. Hiding all functionality permanently
B. Showing essentials first and revealing details when needed
C. Removing help content
D. Displaying every option at once
Answer: B. Showing essentials first and revealing details when needed
Why: It manages complexity by exposing advanced options in context.
Q25. Which is the strongest usability test task?
A. Find and cancel a booked appointment
B. Is the color beautiful?
C. Would you use this app someday?
D. Do you like this screen?
Answer: A. Find and cancel a booked appointment
Why: A realistic task reveals actual behavior rather than relying only on opinions.
Q26. What is an empty state?
A. A full database
B. A failed compile
C. A screen before data or activity exists
D. A server backup
Answer: C. A screen before data or activity exists
Why: Empty states should explain the situation and guide the next useful action.
Q27. Why preserve user input after a validation error?
A. Make recovery impossible
B. Increase frustration
C. Hide the error
D. Avoid forcing users to re-enter correct data
Answer: D. Avoid forcing users to re-enter correct data
Why: Preserving valid entries reduces effort and error recovery time.
Q28. Which UI choice improves form completion?
A. Hide field labels
B. Use unexplained abbreviations
C. Clear all fields on error
D. Show required fields and explain constraints clearly
Answer: D. Show required fields and explain constraints clearly
Why: Clear instructions help users provide correct information on the first attempt.
Q29. What does affordance differ from feedback?
A. Feedback is only for developers
B. Affordance is a test metric
C. They mean exactly the same thing
D. Affordance suggests an action; feedback reports a result
Answer: D. Affordance suggests an action; feedback reports a result
Why: A control's appearance suggests use; feedback tells the user what happened.
Q30. Why evaluate UI with users early?
A. Find interaction problems before they spread into implementation
B. Guarantee every user agrees
C. Avoid all revisions
D. Replace requirements
Answer: A. Find interaction problems before they spread into implementation
Why: Early evaluation catches misunderstandings while design changes are cheaper.
Q31. Users repeatedly make the same input-format error. Which change is most helpful?
A. Hide the field label
B. Add clear constraints and inline validation
C. Use smaller text
D. Remove error messages
Answer: B. Add clear constraints and inline validation
Why: Clear constraints and immediate feedback help users enter valid data.
Q32. What should a good interface provide?
A. Clear feedback after user actions
B. Hidden navigation
C. Unclear labels
D. Unexpected behavior
Answer: A. Clear feedback after user actions
Why: Feedback helps users understand system status.
Q33. Why keep interface controls consistent?
A. Users can transfer what they learn
B. Every page becomes different
C. It prevents all bugs
D. It removes accessibility
Answer: A. Users can transfer what they learn
Why: Consistency makes behavior easier to learn and predict.
Q34. What is accessibility in UI design?
A. Making the interface usable by people with varied abilities
B. Using only bright colors
C. Adding more animations
D. Hiding keyboard controls
Answer: A. Making the interface usable by people with varied abilities
Why: Accessible design supports users with different abilities and needs.
Q35. Which label is clearest for a button?
A. Save changes
B. Thing
C. Do it
D. Option 3
Answer: A. Save changes
Why: Action-oriented labels tell users what will happen.
Q36. What does usability testing observe?
A. Users performing tasks with the interface
B. Only source-code length
C. Only database size
D. Team salary levels
Answer: A. Users performing tasks with the interface
Why: Usability testing reveals how people use and struggle with a product.
Q37. Why show an error message near the problem?
A. Help users identify and correct it
B. Make the page look busy
C. Hide the cause
D. Prevent retries
Answer: A. Help users identify and correct it
Why: Specific, nearby messages make recovery easier.
Q38. Which choice supports readable content?
A. Clear contrast and legible text
B. Tiny text with low contrast
C. Long unexplained labels
D. Color as the only signal
Answer: A. Clear contrast and legible text
Why: Legibility and contrast help users read content.
Q39. What is a prototype in interface design?
A. A model used to explore and test layout or interaction
B. A final database backup
C. A risk register
D. A compiled release only
Answer: A. A model used to explore and test layout or interaction
Why: Prototypes allow early evaluation before full implementation.
Q40. What is a common way to evaluate an interface early?
A. Ask representative users to try a prototype
B. Wait until retirement
C. Remove labels
D. Skip user feedback
Answer: A. Ask representative users to try a prototype
Why: Early usability evaluation reveals interaction problems before release.


9. Software Implementation & Coding
Q1. What is the main benefit of meaningful variable names?
A. They make intent easier to understand
B. They encrypt data
C. They replace tests
D. They guarantee speed
Answer: A. They make intent easier to understand
Why: Names communicate purpose and reduce the effort needed to read code.
Q2. What is a code review intended to find?
A. Only project cost
B. Only user preferences
C. Defects and maintainability issues before merge
D. Only runtime speed
Answer: C. Defects and maintainability issues before merge
Why: Reviewers inspect logic, clarity, security, and consistency.
Q3. What does static analysis do?
A. Examines code without executing it
B. Runs every user workflow
C. Measures customer satisfaction
D. Deploys production
Answer: A. Examines code without executing it
Why: Static analysis can identify patterns such as type issues, unsafe flows, and style violations.
Q4. What is a unit in unit testing?
A. A release schedule
B. A network cable
C. A small testable component or behavior
D. The entire company
Answer: C. A small testable component or behavior
Why: Unit tests focus on a small piece of code in isolation where practical.
Q5. Why use assertions?
A. Hide invalid states
B. Replace every error handler
C. Speed up every algorithm automatically
D. Check assumptions or invariants during execution or tests
Answer: D. Check assumptions or invariants during execution or tests
Why: Assertions detect violated assumptions and expose programming errors.
Q6. What is exception handling for?
A. Responding to exceptional conditions safely
B. Preventing every defect
C. Ignoring all failures
D. Replacing validation
Answer: A. Responding to exceptional conditions safely
Why: Exception handling defines controlled behavior when unexpected conditions occur.
Q7. What is defensive programming?
A. Trust every input
B. Disable all error checks
C. Avoid logging
D. Validate assumptions and handle invalid conditions
Answer: D. Validate assumptions and handle invalid conditions
Why: Defensive techniques reduce damage from invalid inputs and unexpected states.
Q8. Why avoid duplicated code?
A. It prevents defects
B. It always improves maintainability
C. Copies can diverge and require repeated fixes
D. It removes coupling automatically
Answer: C. Copies can diverge and require repeated fixes
Why: One authoritative implementation reduces inconsistent updates.
Q9. What is a code smell?
A. A build artifact
B. A proof of a crash
C. A symptom suggesting deeper code-design trouble
D. A customer request
Answer: C. A symptom suggesting deeper code-design trouble
Why: Smells such as long methods suggest review and possible refactoring.
Q10. What does refactoring preserve?
A. The original file layout
B. All bugs
C. Observable behavior
D. Every internal line exactly
Answer: C. Observable behavior
Why: Refactoring changes internal structure while keeping external behavior stable.
Q11. What is pair programming?
A. Two developers collaborate on one task
B. Two servers share memory
C. A tester writes all code
D. A manager assigns story points
Answer: A. Two developers collaborate on one task
Why: Collaboration can improve review, shared understanding, and problem solving.
Q12. What is a mock object used for?
A. Measuring UI color
B. Compiling source code
C. Replacing production data permanently
D. Simulating a dependency in a test
Answer: D. Simulating a dependency in a test
Why: Mocks isolate a component by controlling interactions with its dependencies.
Q13. Why use a linter?
A. Replace all tests
B. Create requirements
C. Detect style and some common code issues
D. Guarantee algorithmic correctness
Answer: C. Detect style and some common code issues
Why: Linters enforce conventions and flag suspicious patterns.
Q14. What is a race condition?
A. Outcome depends on timing of concurrent operations
B. A syntax error
C. A planned release
D. A slow user interface
Answer: A. Outcome depends on timing of concurrent operations
Why: Uncontrolled interleavings can cause inconsistent or unpredictable results.
Q15. Why avoid hard-coded secrets?
A. They cannot be recovered
B. They can leak through source or build artifacts
C. They improve secret rotation
D. They are safer than a vault
Answer: B. They can leak through source or build artifacts
Why: Secrets should be managed through secure configuration or secret stores.
Q16. What is input validation?
A. Encrypting every output
B. Renaming variables
C. Checking data against expected rules before use
D. Running a release
Answer: C. Checking data against expected rules before use
Why: Validation rejects or handles malformed or out-of-range input.
Q17. What does immutability help with?
A. Disabling tests
B. Reducing unintended state changes
C. Increasing shared mutable state
D. Removing all types
Answer: B. Reducing unintended state changes
Why: Immutable values are easier to reason about, especially in concurrent code.
Q18. What is a compiler's role?
A. Translate source code and report compile-time issues
B. Gather user requirements
C. Approve project scope
D. Run usability studies
Answer: A. Translate source code and report compile-time issues
Why: A compiler translates code into another representation and detects certain errors.
Q19. What is a build artifact?
A. A risk owner
B. A user persona
C. A stakeholder interview
D. Output produced by the build process
Answer: D. Output produced by the build process
Why: Artifacts include executables, packages, libraries, and generated files.
Q20. Why automate builds?
A. Avoid version control
B. Make build steps repeatable and reduce manual errors
C. Guarantee no bugs
D. Remove code review
Answer: B. Make build steps repeatable and reduce manual errors
Why: Automated builds improve consistency and repeatability.
Q21. What is an API contract?
A. Defined operations, inputs, outputs, and behavior
B. A meeting agenda
C. A user password
D. A UI theme
Answer: A. Defined operations, inputs, outputs, and behavior
Why: Contracts let components integrate against stable expectations.
Q22. What is code readability?
A. How easily people can understand the code
B. How many files are shipped
C. How many lines exist
D. How fast the CPU runs
Answer: A. How easily people can understand the code
Why: Readable code reduces maintenance effort and review mistakes.
Q23. Why handle errors near the right abstraction level?
A. Provide useful recovery without hiding important failures
B. Silence every exception
C. Repeat the same message everywhere
D. Avoid logging
Answer: A. Provide useful recovery without hiding important failures
Why: Errors should be handled where meaningful recovery or context is available.
Q24. What is dependency injection?
A. Deleting interfaces
B. Avoiding tests
C. Providing dependencies from outside a component
D. Hard-coding every dependency inside
