Answer: C. Providing dependencies from outside a component
Why: Injection decouples construction from use and makes substitution easier.
Q25. What is a deadlock in concurrent code?
A. A method returns normally
B. A test is skipped
C. Threads wait indefinitely on resources held by one another
D. A variable is immutable
Answer: C. Threads wait indefinitely on resources held by one another
Why: Circular waiting can prevent all involved threads from progressing.
Q26. What is secure coding?
A. Only adding encryption at the end
B. Hiding all errors from developers
C. Skipping input checks
D. Writing code to avoid exploitable weaknesses
Answer: D. Writing code to avoid exploitable weaknesses
Why: Secure coding includes validation, safe APIs, access control, and careful error handling.
Q27. Why keep functions small and focused?
A. They are easier to understand and test
B. They guarantee zero bugs
C. They remove all interfaces
D. They always use less memory
Answer: A. They are easier to understand and test
Why: Focused functions are easier to reason about and verify.
Q28. What is a code formatter for?
A. Managing project risks
B. Applying consistent code layout automatically
C. Finding every logic error
D. Running load tests
Answer: B. Applying consistent code layout automatically
Why: Formatters reduce style debates and keep layout consistent.
Q29. What does continuous integration encourage?
A. Separate unintegrated code forever
B. Frequent merging with automated build and tests
C. One merge at project end
D. No automated checks
Answer: B. Frequent merging with automated build and tests
Why: Frequent integration reveals conflicts and failures early.
Q30. Why is code ownership useful?
A. It prevents code review
B. It removes documentation
C. It clarifies responsibility while still allowing collaboration
D. It guarantees no turnover
Answer: C. It clarifies responsibility while still allowing collaboration
Why: Ownership helps identify maintainers and accountability for critical components.
Q31. A function has many nested conditions and is difficult to review. What is the best improvement?
A. Add more global variables
B. Split the logic into small, well-named functions
C. Remove all tests
D. Duplicate the function
Answer: B. Split the logic into small, well-named functions
Why: Smaller functions make logic easier to understand, test, and maintain.
Q32. What is the purpose of a code review?
A. Find defects and improve code quality
B. Replace all tests
C. Guarantee no future changes
D. Set project prices
Answer: A. Find defects and improve code quality
Why: Reviewers can identify defects, maintainability issues, and unclear logic.
Q33. Why use meaningful variable names?
A. Make code easier to understand
B. Increase ambiguity
C. Prevent compilation
D. Replace documentation entirely
Answer: A. Make code easier to understand
Why: Clear names communicate intent to readers.
Q34. What is a coding standard?
A. Agreed rules for writing consistent code
B. A customer invoice
C. A deployment outage
D. A project charter
Answer: A. Agreed rules for writing consistent code
Why: Standards improve consistency and maintainability.
Q35. What does a compiler commonly do?
A. Translates source code into another form and reports errors
B. Interviews stakeholders
C. Plans a sprint
D. Draws user journeys
Answer: A. Translates source code into another form and reports errors
Why: Compilers translate code and detect certain errors.
Q36. Why avoid duplicated logic?
A. A fix may otherwise need to be repeated
B. It always improves reliability
C. It removes dependencies automatically
D. It prevents reuse
Answer: A. A fix may otherwise need to be repeated
Why: Duplicated logic increases maintenance effort and inconsistency risk.
Q37. What is defensive programming?
A. Checking assumptions and handling invalid inputs
B. Ignoring errors
C. Removing validation
D. Using unclear names
Answer: A. Checking assumptions and handling invalid inputs
Why: Defensive checks help software respond safely to unexpected conditions.
Q38. What does version control help developers do?
A. Track and manage source-code changes
B. Measure user satisfaction directly
C. Replace all testing
D. Guarantee perfect requirements
Answer: A. Track and manage source-code changes
Why: Version control records history and supports collaboration.
Q39. Why keep functions reasonably small and focused?
A. They are easier to understand and test
B. They remove all need for design
C. They guarantee zero bugs
D. They increase hidden dependencies
Answer: A. They are easier to understand and test
Why: Focused functions are generally easier to reason about and verify.
Q40. What is a useful purpose of exception handling?
A. Respond to errors in a controlled way
B. Hide every failure
C. Remove input checks
D. Replace all tests
Answer: A. Respond to errors in a controlled way
Why: Good error handling helps software fail safely and clearly.


10. Software Testing
Q1. What is the main goal of software testing?
A. Replace requirements
B. Find failures and assess quality
C. Guarantee future reliability
D. Prove no defects exist
Answer: B. Find failures and assess quality
Why: Testing provides evidence about behavior and reveals defects, but cannot prove total absence of defects.
Q2. A test checks one function in isolation. It is a:
A. System test
B. Acceptance test
C. Unit test
D. Site test
Answer: C. Unit test
Why: Unit tests focus on small components.
Q3. Testing interactions between modules is:
A. Acceptance testing only
B. Usability research
C. Unit testing only
D. Integration testing
Answer: D. Integration testing
Why: Integration testing checks interfaces and behavior across combined components.
Q4. Testing the complete integrated product is:
A. System testing
B. Unit testing
C. Static analysis
D. Code formatting
Answer: A. System testing
Why: System testing evaluates the whole system against requirements.
Q5. Who commonly performs acceptance testing?
A. Customer or representative users
B. Only build server
C. Only database
D. Only compiler
Answer: A. Customer or representative users
Why: Acceptance testing determines whether the product meets agreed acceptance needs.
Q6. What is regression testing?
A. Measuring team morale
B. Checking that changes did not break existing behavior
C. Testing only brand-new features
D. Testing before any code exists
Answer: B. Checking that changes did not break existing behavior
Why: Regression tests rerun relevant checks after changes.
Q7. Which technique tests input boundaries?
A. Code ownership
B. Random UI styling
C. Boundary value analysis
D. Risk transfer
Answer: C. Boundary value analysis
Why: Defects often occur at minimum, maximum, and just-inside/outside boundaries.
Q8. For input range 1–100, which is a useful boundary set?
A. 20, 30, 40, 50
B. 0, 1, 100, 101
C. 10, 20, 30, 40
D. 2, 25, 75, 99 only
Answer: B. 0, 1, 100, 101
Why: These values test just outside and exactly at both boundaries.
Q9. Equivalence partitioning divides inputs into:
A. Release branches
B. Development teams
C. Random source files
D. Groups expected to behave similarly
Answer: D. Groups expected to behave similarly
Why: Representative values can be selected from valid and invalid classes.
Q10. What is a test oracle?
A. A test environment
B. A release manager
C. A code formatter
D. A source of expected results
Answer: D. A source of expected results
Why: An oracle tells the tester what result should be expected.
Q11. What does statement coverage measure?
A. Defects in production only
B. Number of users
C. Correctness of all requirements
D. Executed statements during tests
Answer: D. Executed statements during tests
Why: Statement coverage indicates which executable statements were run.
Q12. 100% statement coverage guarantees no defects. This claim is:
A. True if code compiles
B. True
C. False
D. True only for large systems
Answer: C. False
Why: Coverage does not guarantee all paths, conditions, or expected behaviors are correct.
Q13. What is a test stub?
A. A simplified component that a tested module calls
B. A release note
C. A project risk
D. A real production database always
Answer: A. A simplified component that a tested module calls
Why: Stubs provide controlled responses for dependencies called by the unit under test.
Q14. What is a test driver?
A. A database backup
B. A user persona
C. A code review checklist
D. A component that calls the tested module
Answer: D. A component that calls the tested module
Why: Drivers invoke a component when the real caller is not available.
Q15. What is exploratory testing?
A. Running only a fixed script
B. Learning, designing, and executing tests together
C. Avoiding observation
D. Testing only compile errors
Answer: B. Learning, designing, and executing tests together
Why: Exploratory testing uses ongoing learning to guide further tests.
Q16. What is smoke testing?
A. A broad, shallow check that a build is stable enough for further testing
B. An exhaustive security audit
C. A final user survey
D. A code style review
Answer: A. A broad, shallow check that a build is stable enough for further testing
Why: Smoke tests quickly identify major build or environment failures.
Q17. What is sanity testing often used for?
A. A focused check of a specific change or fix
B. Testing every feature exhaustively
C. Checking project budgets
D. Replacing all regression tests
Answer: A. A focused check of a specific change or fix
Why: Sanity testing gives a quick confidence check around a limited area.
Q18. What is a flaky test?
A. A manual test
B. A test that passes and fails inconsistently without relevant code changes
C. A test that always fails for a clear defect
D. A test with a long name
Answer: B. A test that passes and fails inconsistently without relevant code changes
Why: Flakiness can arise from timing, shared state, or unstable environments.
Q19. Why use test data management?
A. Replace test design
B. Avoid resetting environments
C. Share real sensitive data freely
D. Keep test data controlled, repeatable, and appropriate
Answer: D. Keep test data controlled, repeatable, and appropriate
Why: Controlled data improves repeatability and protects privacy.
Q20. What is a severity rating?
A. The cost of a developer's laptop
B. How serious the defect's impact is
C. How soon the tester found it only
D. How long the test name is
Answer: B. How serious the defect's impact is
Why: Severity reflects the impact of a failure on users or operations.
Q21. What is defect priority?
A. The test's color
B. The age of the tester
C. The number of lines in the file
D. How urgently the defect should be fixed
Answer: D. How urgently the defect should be fixed
Why: Priority reflects scheduling urgency and business importance.
Q22. What is the purpose of a test plan?
A. Define scope, approach, resources, and schedule for testing
B. Replace requirements
C. List only source files
D. Guarantee zero defects
Answer: A. Define scope, approach, resources, and schedule for testing
Why: A plan communicates what will be tested and how testing will be managed.
Q23. What is a negative test?
A. Checks behavior with invalid or unexpected inputs
B. Tests only documentation
C. Tests only performance
D. Checks only the ideal path
Answer: A. Checks behavior with invalid or unexpected inputs
Why: Negative tests verify safe handling of invalid conditions.
Q24. What is load testing?
A. Measure usability only
B. Evaluate behavior under expected workload
C. Review class names
D. Check only password rules
Answer: B. Evaluate behavior under expected workload
Why: Load testing measures performance under anticipated traffic or work volume.
Q25. What is stress testing?
A. Verify variable naming
B. Push the system beyond normal limits to observe behavior
C. Review the contract
D. Test only the first screen
Answer: B. Push the system beyond normal limits to observe behavior
Why: Stress tests explore limits, failure modes, and recovery.
Q26. What does a test environment include?
A. Only a tester's name
B. Only the project charter
C. Only requirements
D. Required hardware, software, configuration, and data
Answer: D. Required hardware, software, configuration, and data
Why: Environment details can affect test reproducibility and results.
Q27. What is a defect life cycle?
A. A deployment topology
B. A coding style guide
C. A software process model
D. States a defect passes through from reporting to closure
Answer: D. States a defect passes through from reporting to closure
Why: Tracking states helps manage triage, fixing, retesting, and closure.
Q28. What is the purpose of retesting a fixed defect?
A. Confirm the specific failure is corrected
B. Prove unrelated features are safe
C. Estimate project cost
D. Replace regression testing entirely
Answer: A. Confirm the specific failure is corrected
Why: Retesting verifies the reported issue no longer occurs.
Q29. When should testing stop?
A. When agreed exit criteria and risk decisions support stopping
B. Whenever the developer is tired
C. When the first test passes
D. Only when no test fails ever
Answer: A. When agreed exit criteria and risk decisions support stopping
Why: Exit decisions use coverage, defect status, time, and residual risk rather than impossible certainty.
Q30. What is mutation testing used to assess?
A. Whether UI colors match
B. Whether tests detect small injected code changes
C. Whether requirements are signed
D. Whether deployment is fast
Answer: B. Whether tests detect small injected code changes
Why: Mutation testing evaluates test-suite effectiveness by checking if tests catch altered behavior.
Q31. A test checks that a valid user can reset a forgotten password. What is its main focus?
A. Expected user-visible behavior
B. Source-code formatting
C. Developer attendance
D. Hardware purchasing
Answer: A. Expected user-visible behavior
Why: The test verifies the feature from the user or functional perspective.
Q32. What does unit testing usually test?
A. A small component in isolation
B. The whole organization
C. Only user satisfaction
D. The project budget
Answer: A. A small component in isolation
Why: Unit tests check individual functions or components.
Q33. What does integration testing focus on?
A. Interactions between components
B. Only one line of code
C. Staff performance
D. Project scope
Answer: A. Interactions between components
Why: Integration tests find issues at component boundaries.
Q34. What is regression testing?
A. Checking existing behavior after changes
B. Testing only new users
C. Estimating cost
D. Designing a logo
Answer: A. Checking existing behavior after changes
Why: Regression tests detect unintended effects of changes.
Q35. What is a test case made from?
A. Inputs, conditions, actions, and expected results
B. Only a project name
C. Only source comments
D. A meeting agenda
Answer: A. Inputs, conditions, actions, and expected results
Why: A test case defines how to check a behavior and its expected outcome.
Q36. What is black-box testing based on?
A. External behavior and specifications
B. Internal code structure only
C. Developer seniority
D. Variable names only
Answer: A. External behavior and specifications
Why: Black-box tests assess observable behavior without relying on internal implementation.
Q37. What does code coverage measure?
A. How much code is exercised by tests
B. The number of users
C. The budget used
D. The speed of typing
Answer: A. How much code is exercised by tests
Why: Coverage indicates which code was executed by tests, not whether all bugs are found.
Q38. When is acceptance testing often performed?
A. To determine whether agreed user needs are met
B. Only before requirements exist
C. Instead of all design
D. Only during hiring
Answer: A. To determine whether agreed user needs are met
Why: Acceptance testing evaluates the system against agreed acceptance conditions.
Q39. Why use both automated and exploratory testing?
A. They provide complementary ways to find problems
B. They guarantee no defects
C. They remove the need for requirements
D. They test exactly the same things always
Answer: A. They provide complementary ways to find problems
Why: Automation repeats checks efficiently while exploration can uncover unexpected issues.
Q40. What is the purpose of a test oracle?
A. Determine the expected result of a test
B. Assign developer salaries
C. Create a schedule
D. Choose architecture style
Answer: A. Determine the expected result of a test
Why: A test oracle provides the basis for judging actual results.


11. Software Maintenance & Evolution
Q1. Fixing a production calculation error is:
A. Adaptive maintenance
B. Perfective maintenance
C. Preventive maintenance
D. Corrective maintenance
Answer: D. Corrective maintenance
Why: Corrective maintenance removes faults found after delivery.
Q2. Updating software for a new operating system is:
A. Acceptance testing
B. Corrective maintenance
C. Retirement
D. Adaptive maintenance
Answer: D. Adaptive maintenance
Why: Adaptive maintenance responds to environmental changes.
Q3. Improving report usability after release is:
A. Configuration audit
B. Corrective maintenance
C. Perfective maintenance
D. Risk avoidance
Answer: C. Perfective maintenance
Why: Perfective maintenance enhances features or performance based on needs.
Q4. Restructuring fragile code to reduce future faults is:
A. Deployment
B. Only corrective maintenance
C. Requirements elicitation
D. Preventive maintenance
Answer: D. Preventive maintenance
Why: Preventive maintenance improves future maintainability and reliability.
Q5. What is legacy software?
A. A future requirement
B. A test stub
C. Existing software still used, often with older technologies
D. Only brand-new code
Answer: C. Existing software still used, often with older technologies
Why: Legacy systems may remain valuable despite outdated platforms or difficult maintenance.
Q6. What is program comprehension?
A. Estimating salaries
B. Creating a logo
C. Understanding existing code and behavior
D. Compiling without reading
Answer: C. Understanding existing code and behavior
Why: Maintainers need to understand how current behavior and dependencies work.
Q7. What is reverse engineering?
A. Deriving higher-level design or information from an existing system
B. Deleting old software
C. Building only from new requirements
D. Running acceptance tests
Answer: A. Deriving higher-level design or information from an existing system
Why: Reverse engineering recovers structure and knowledge from existing artifacts.
Q8. What is reengineering?
A. Closing a risk
B. Analyzing and transforming an existing system to improve it
C. Testing one function
D. Only writing a new user manual
Answer: B. Analyzing and transforming an existing system to improve it
Why: Reengineering modernizes or restructures a system while preserving needed behavior.
Q9. Why is regression testing important during maintenance?
A. Changes may break previously working behavior
B. It guarantees zero future defects
C. It replaces change review
D. Maintenance never affects other features
Answer: A. Changes may break previously working behavior
Why: Dependencies mean a local change can cause failures elsewhere.
Q10. What is software erosion?
A. Increasing difficulty of change as structure degrades over time
B. A testing technique
C. A planned release
D. A user persona
Answer: A. Increasing difficulty of change as structure degrades over time
Why: Uncontrolled changes can weaken architecture and make maintenance harder.
Q11. What is a patch?
A. A UML diagram
B. A full project charter
C. A limited change addressing a defect or issue
D. A risk matrix
Answer: C. A limited change addressing a defect or issue
Why: Patches deliver targeted corrections or updates.
Q12. What should be assessed before changing legacy code?
A. Only the variable colors
B. Only the developer's age
C. Dependencies, side effects, and regression risk
D. Nothing if it compiles
Answer: C. Dependencies, side effects, and regression risk
Why: Impact analysis helps identify affected modules and tests.
Q13. Why retain historical change records?
A. Replace source code
B. Prevent all future change
C. Understand why behavior changed and support diagnosis
D. Guarantee compliance automatically
Answer: C. Understand why behavior changed and support diagnosis
Why: History supports debugging, audits, and future maintenance decisions.
Q14. What is technical debt repayment in maintenance?
A. Adding more shortcuts
B. Ignoring architecture
C. Deleting all tests
D. Refactoring or redesigning costly shortcuts
Answer: D. Refactoring or redesigning costly shortcuts
Why: Repayment reduces future change cost caused by earlier compromises.
Q15. What is a maintenance window?
A. Planned time when updates or downtime may occur
B. A testing framework
C. A source-code branch
D. A UI popup
Answer: A. Planned time when updates or downtime may occur
Why: A maintenance window coordinates operational impact and user expectations.
Q16. Why might a system be retired?
A. It uses modules
B. It passed all tests
C. It has documentation
D. Its cost, risk, or business value no longer justifies continued operation
Answer: D. Its cost, risk, or business value no longer justifies continued operation
Why: Retirement decisions consider value, support, risk, and replacement options.
Q17. What is data migration risk during replacement?
A. Data may be lost, corrupted, or mapped incorrectly
B. Tests run faster automatically
C. Scope becomes fixed
D. UI labels become consistent
Answer: A. Data may be lost, corrupted, or mapped incorrectly
Why: Migration requires mapping, validation, backup, and reconciliation.
Q18. What is a maintenance backlog?
A. Only completed work
B. Known fixes and improvements awaiting prioritization
C. A project logo
D. A compiled binary
Answer: B. Known fixes and improvements awaiting prioritization
Why: It records outstanding changes to be assessed and scheduled.
Q19. What is change impact analysis?
A. Estimating only screen size
B. Deleting old releases
C. Changing code without review
D. Finding components, tests, and users affected by a change
Answer: D. Finding components, tests, and users affected by a change
Why: It identifies consequences before implementation.
Q20. Why automate regression suites for frequently maintained systems?
A. Manual testing becomes illegal
B. All defects disappear
C. Repeated checks become faster and more consistent
D. Requirements stop changing
Answer: C. Repeated checks become faster and more consistent
Why: Automation makes repeated validation more practical after each change.
Q21. What is a hotfix?
A. A planned annual redesign
B. An urgent fix delivered outside the normal release cadence
C. A risk category
D. A UI prototype
Answer: B. An urgent fix delivered outside the normal release cadence
Why: Hotfixes address urgent production issues and still need controlled validation.
Q22. Why keep a rollback plan?
A. Replace monitoring
B. Avoid backups
C. Restore a known working version if release fails
D. Increase deployment uncertainty
Answer: C. Restore a known working version if release fails
Why: Rollback limits service disruption if an update causes serious problems.
Q23. What does maintainability index attempt to represent?
A. A composite estimate of maintainability-related code properties
B. The number of users online
C. The project budget only
D. The number of releases
Answer: A. A composite estimate of maintainability-related code properties
Why: Such indices approximate maintainability using factors like complexity and size; interpretation varies.
Q24. What is a dependency upgrade risk?
A. All tests become irrelevant
B. Documentation is always deleted
C. Upgrades never affect behavior
D. New versions may change behavior or introduce incompatibilities
Answer: D. New versions may change behavior or introduce incompatibilities
Why: Compatibility and security changes need evaluation and testing.
Q25. Why document workarounds in legacy systems?
A. They explain unusual behavior and prevent repeated investigation
B. They replace source control
C. They stop user feedback
D. They guarantee no technical debt
Answer: A. They explain unusual behavior and prevent repeated investigation
Why: Workaround knowledge can be critical when behavior is non-obvious.
Q26. What is software adaptability?
A. Number of classes
B. The time to hire staff
C. Ease of printing
D. Ability to adjust to new environments or requirements
Answer: D. Ability to adjust to new environments or requirements
Why: Adaptability reflects how readily software can be changed for new conditions.
Q27. What is the danger of modifying code without tests?
A. Regressions may go unnoticed
B. Changes become reversible by default
C. Requirements become clearer
D. The code becomes automatically secure
Answer: A. Regressions may go unnoticed
Why: Without suitable tests, maintainers have less evidence that behavior remains correct.
Q28. What is a migration rehearsal?
A. A final customer invoice
B. A code formatting rule
C. A new risk score
D. A trial run of moving data or systems before the real cutover
Answer: D. A trial run of moving data or systems before the real cutover
Why: Rehearsals expose timing and data problems before production migration.
Q29. Which maintenance decision is best when a small fix threatens a critical system?
A. Assess risk, test in a safe environment, and plan rollback
B. Skip impact analysis
C. Ignore operational staff
D. Edit production directly without backup
Answer: A. Assess risk, test in a safe environment, and plan rollback
Why: Controlled validation and recovery planning reduce the impact of maintenance failure.
Q30. What does end-of-life mean for a software product?
A. Official support or maintenance is ending
B. All data is automatically erased
C. The source code is always public
D. The product has no users
Answer: A. Official support or maintenance is ending
Why: End-of-life signals a support boundary and may require migration planning.
Q31. A change is made to fix a defect, and related features are retested. What type of maintenance triggered the change?
A. Corrective
B. Perfective
C. Preventive
D. Adaptive
Answer: A. Corrective
Why: Corrective maintenance addresses faults discovered in software.
Q32. What is corrective maintenance?
A. Fixing a defect after delivery
B. Adapting to a new platform
C. Improving future structure only
D. Retiring a product
Answer: A. Fixing a defect after delivery
Why: Corrective maintenance addresses faults found in delivered software.
Q33. What is adaptive maintenance?
A. Changing software for a new environment
B. Fixing every typo only
C. Adding no changes
D. Deleting tests
Answer: A. Changing software for a new environment
Why: Adaptive maintenance responds to environmental changes.
Q34. What is perfective maintenance?
A. Improving performance or adding useful enhancements
B. Fixing only crashes
C. Moving to a new operating system only
D. Removing documentation
Answer: A. Improving performance or adding useful enhancements
Why: Perfective maintenance improves features or performance.
Q35. What is preventive maintenance?
A. Reducing future failure or maintenance risk
B. Adding random features
C. Avoiding code review
D. Deleting version history
Answer: A. Reducing future failure or maintenance risk
Why: Preventive changes improve future maintainability or reliability.
Q36. Why is legacy software sometimes hard to change?
A. Knowledge and documentation may be limited
B. It always has no users
C. It cannot run code
D. It never contains dependencies
Answer: A. Knowledge and documentation may be limited
Why: Old systems may have outdated designs, limited tests, or missing knowledge.
Q37. What is refactoring useful for during evolution?
A. Improving internal structure while preserving behavior
B. Changing user needs without review
C. Removing regression tests
D. Guaranteeing no defects
Answer: A. Improving internal structure while preserving behavior
Why: Refactoring makes future changes safer and easier.
Q38. What is software retirement?
A. Taking a system out of service
B. Adding a new feature
C. Testing a single function
D. Creating a prototype
Answer: A. Taking a system out of service
Why: Retirement removes a system from operational use in a planned way.
Q39. Why run regression tests after maintenance?
A. Check that changes did not break existing features
B. Replace impact analysis
C. Avoid reviewing code
D. Prove no defect exists
Answer: A. Check that changes did not break existing features
Why: Maintenance changes can affect previously working behavior.
Q40. What should be assessed before changing a legacy component?
A. Impact on dependent components and behavior
B. Only its file name
C. Only the screen color
D. Nothing if it compiles
Answer: A. Impact on dependent components and behavior
Why: Impact analysis helps reveal possible side effects of maintenance.


12. Software Quality Assurance
Q1. What is the main focus of Software Quality Assurance (SQA)?
A. Only fixing one bug
B. Only selling the product
C. Only writing code
D. Confidence that processes and products follow quality practices
Answer: D. Confidence that processes and products follow quality practices
Why: SQA focuses on planned processes and activities that support quality.
Q2. How does QA differ from QC?
A. QC means planning only
B. QA emphasizes processes; QC evaluates product outputs
C. QA means coding only
D. They are always identical
Answer: B. QA emphasizes processes; QC evaluates product outputs
Why: Quality assurance is process-oriented, while quality control checks deliverables.
Q3. What is a quality audit?
A. A systematic check against defined standards or procedures
B. A project estimate
C. A user interface sketch
D. A code compiler
Answer: A. A systematic check against defined standards or procedures
Why: Audits gather evidence of compliance with requirements or processes.
Q4. What is a defect prevention activity?
A. Deleting defect reports
B. Skipping reviews
C. Root-cause analysis and process improvement
D. Ignoring recurring failures
Answer: C. Root-cause analysis and process improvement
Why: Prevention addresses causes so similar defects are less likely to recur.
Q5. What is a quality plan?
A. Replaces the product requirements
B. Lists only salaries
C. Defines quality goals, standards, responsibilities, and checks
D. Guarantees no defects
Answer: C. Defines quality goals, standards, responsibilities, and checks
Why: A plan specifies how quality will be achieved and assessed.
Q6. What is a root cause?
A. A release date
B. The last person who saw it
C. A test's name
D. Underlying reason a problem occurred
Answer: D. Underlying reason a problem occurred
Why: Root-cause analysis looks beyond symptoms to contributing system conditions.
Q7. What does a Pareto chart help identify?
A. The project charter
B. A small number of categories causing many problems
C. All possible defects
D. The best UI color
Answer: B. A small number of categories causing many problems
Why: It ranks categories to help focus improvement on high-impact causes.
Q8. What is a fishbone diagram used for?
A. Showing release dates
B. Running tests
C. Organizing possible causes of a problem
D. Showing class inheritance
Answer: C. Organizing possible causes of a problem
Why: Cause-and-effect diagrams structure brainstorming around potential causes.
Q9. What is a process standard?
A. An agreed way of performing or evaluating work
B. A user password
C. A random developer preference
D. A production defect
Answer: A. An agreed way of performing or evaluating work
Why: Standards make expectations consistent and auditable.
Q10. Why use peer reviews?
A. Avoid shared knowledge
B. Find issues early through independent inspection
C. Replace all dynamic tests
D. Guarantee all bugs disappear
Answer: B. Find issues early through independent inspection
Why: Reviews catch defects and improve consistency before execution or release.
Q11. What is a nonconformity?
A. A user story
B. A passing test
C. A planned feature
D. Failure to meet a specified requirement or standard
Answer: D. Failure to meet a specified requirement or standard
Why: Nonconformities require assessment and, where appropriate, corrective action.
Q12. What is corrective action?
A. Only hiding the symptom
B. Changing the logo
C. Skipping verification
D. Addressing the cause of a detected problem
Answer: D. Addressing the cause of a detected problem
Why: Corrective action aims to prevent recurrence by dealing with the cause.
Q13. What is preventive action?
A. Closing all risks without analysis
B. Addressing a potential problem before it occurs
C. Fixing only an already failed test
D. Removing standards
Answer: B. Addressing a potential problem before it occurs
Why: Preventive action reduces the chance of future nonconformities.
Q14. What is a quality gate?
A. A defined checkpoint with criteria for proceeding
B. A customer survey
C. A login screen
D. A code branch
Answer: A. A defined checkpoint with criteria for proceeding
Why: Quality gates stop progression until agreed conditions are satisfied.
Q15. Why track defect trends?
A. Replace risk management
B. Guarantee every defect is known
C. Count employees
D. Detect recurring weaknesses and evaluate improvements
Answer: D. Detect recurring weaknesses and evaluate improvements
Why: Trends can reveal hotspots and whether corrective actions help.
Q16. What is process compliance?
A. Following applicable approved procedures and standards
B. Writing more code
C. Avoiding documentation
D. Passing every test automatically
Answer: A. Following applicable approved procedures and standards
Why: Compliance means required practices are followed and evidenced.
Q17. What is continuous improvement?
A. Freezing every process
B. Repeatedly measuring and improving work processes
C. Avoiding feedback
D. Making one change and never reviewing it
Answer: B. Repeatedly measuring and improving work processes
Why: Improvement uses evidence and feedback in an ongoing cycle.
Q18. Which evidence best supports a quality claim?
A. A verbal promise alone
B. Recorded test results and review findings
C. An unverified estimate
D. A logo
Answer: B. Recorded test results and review findings
Why: Objective evidence makes quality decisions more reliable.
Q19. What is a checklist useful for in reviews?
A. Proving all defects are absent
B. Ensuring common issues are considered consistently
C. Replacing reviewer judgment entirely
D. Removing standards
Answer: B. Ensuring common issues are considered consistently
Why: Checklists help reviewers remember frequent risk areas.
Q20. What is quality cost of prevention?
A. Effort spent avoiding defects before they occur
B. Server response time
C. Revenue from a new feature
D. Cost of repairing a customer claim only
Answer: A. Effort spent avoiding defects before they occur
Why: Prevention costs include training, process improvement, and early quality planning.
Q21. What is appraisal cost?
A. Cost of ignoring a defect
B. Only customer refund cost
C. Cost of evaluating whether quality requirements are met
D. Project profit
Answer: C. Cost of evaluating whether quality requirements are met
Why: Appraisal includes inspection, testing, and quality audits.
Q22. What are internal failure costs?
A. Planning costs
B. Costs of defects found only by customers
C. Costs of defects found before delivery
D. Training costs
Answer: C. Costs of defects found before delivery
Why: Internal failures include rework and retesting before release.
Q23. What are external failure costs?
A. Requirements workshops
B. Code review effort
C. Prevention training
D. Costs from defects found after delivery
Answer: D. Costs from defects found after delivery
Why: External failures can include support, outages, refunds, and reputational harm.
Q24. Why is independence valuable in an audit?
A. It guarantees agreement
B. It eliminates standards
C. It reduces bias and improves objectivity
D. It removes the need for evidence
Answer: C. It reduces bias and improves objectivity
Why: Independent reviewers may identify issues overlooked by those who created the work.
Q25. What is a quality attribute scenario?
A. A team roster
B. A random requirement
C. A source-code branch
D. A specific, testable statement of a quality response under conditions
Answer: D. A specific, testable statement of a quality response under conditions
Why: Scenarios make quality expectations concrete and evaluable.
Q26. Why should quality responsibilities be clear?
A. It prevents communication
B. Teams know who plans, performs, and verifies checks
C. Only QA needs to care about quality
D. It removes accountability
Answer: B. Teams know who plans, performs, and verifies checks
Why: Clear ownership helps quality activities happen at the right time.
Q27. What does ISO 9001 relate to broadly?
A. Quality management systems
B. A test case format
C. A programming language
D. A database engine
Answer: A. Quality management systems
Why: ISO 9001 specifies requirements for a quality management system.
Q28. What is the purpose of a retrospective for quality?
A. Delete defects
B. Avoid metrics
C. Identify process changes that may prevent recurring issues
D. Assign blame only
Answer: C. Identify process changes that may prevent recurring issues
Why: Retrospectives help teams learn and improve their working practices.
Q29. Why is quality not only the tester's responsibility?
A. Testing guarantees perfection
B. Quality exists only after release
C. Testers write every requirement
D. Requirements, design, coding, and operations all affect quality
Answer: D. Requirements, design, coding, and operations all affect quality
Why: Quality is influenced throughout the lifecycle, so everyone contributes.
Q30. What should follow an audit finding?
A. Ignore it if release is near
B. Delete the audit record
C. Document evidence, assess impact, and track corrective action
D. Change standards secretly
Answer: C. Document evidence, assess impact, and track corrective action
Why: Findings need ownership and follow-up to ensure issues are resolved.
Q31. Which activity is primarily process-focused rather than product-testing-focused?
A. Running a regression suite
B. Auditing whether teams follow the defined development process
C. Measuring response time
D. Checking one output value
Answer: B. Auditing whether teams follow the defined development process
Why: A process audit checks adherence to standards and procedures.
Q32. What is the purpose of quality assurance?
A. Improve processes to support quality
B. Only find defects after release
C. Replace all requirements
D. Guarantee zero cost
Answer: A. Improve processes to support quality
Why: QA emphasizes planned processes that help prevent quality problems.
Q33. What is the difference between QA and quality control?
A. QA focuses on processes; QC checks work products
B. They always mean exactly the same thing
C. QC replaces development
D. QA only counts users
Answer: A. QA focuses on processes; QC checks work products
Why: QA improves the process while QC evaluates outputs for defects.
Q34. What is a quality audit?
A. A systematic check against defined procedures or standards
B. A coding sprint
C. A UI prototype
D. A customer login
Answer: A. A systematic check against defined procedures or standards
Why: Audits assess whether required practices and controls are followed.
Q35. Why establish quality standards?
A. Provide consistent expectations for work
B. Prevent every project change
C. Remove testing
D. Choose variable names only
Answer: A. Provide consistent expectations for work
Why: Standards help teams apply consistent quality criteria.
Q36. What is a defect prevention activity?
A. Reviewing requirements before implementation
B. Ignoring recurring errors
C. Skipping design
D. Hiding test results
Answer: A. Reviewing requirements before implementation
Why: Early reviews can identify ambiguity and omissions before they spread.
Q37. What does a nonconformance report record?
A. A failure to meet a specified requirement or process
B. A successful login only
C. A project celebration
D. A list of colors
Answer: A. A failure to meet a specified requirement or process
Why: Nonconformance records help track and resolve departures from requirements.
Q38. Why analyze recurring defects?
A. Find root causes and prevent repetition
B. Assign blame only
C. Delete the defect log
D. Avoid process improvement
Answer: A. Find root causes and prevent repetition
Why: Root-cause analysis helps address systemic problems.
Q39. What is continuous improvement?
A. Regularly evaluating and improving processes
B. Never changing a process
C. Testing only at the end
D. Removing all measurements
Answer: A. Regularly evaluating and improving processes
Why: Continuous improvement uses evidence and feedback to improve outcomes.
Q40. What is a quality checklist used for?
A. Check work against agreed criteria
B. Replace every test
C. Hide defects
D. Set project scope without approval
Answer: A. Check work against agreed criteria
Why: Checklists help reviewers apply quality criteria consistently.


13. Software Metrics & Measurement
Q1. A metric is best described as:
A. A quantitative measure of an attribute
B. A deployment server
C. A personal opinion only
D. A design pattern
Answer: A. A quantitative measure of an attribute
Why: Metrics quantify properties such as defects, effort, size, or response time.
Q2. What is the difference between measure and metric?
A. A metric is never numeric
B. They always mean exactly the same thing
C. A measure is a value; a metric often relates or interprets measures
D. A measure is always a forecast
Answer: C. A measure is a value; a metric often relates or interprets measures
Why: Metrics are often derived or interpreted measures used for a specific purpose.
Q3. Which is a size measure?
A. Mean time to repair
B. Customer satisfaction only
C. Availability percentage
D. Lines of code
Answer: D. Lines of code
Why: LOC is a size measure, although it has limitations across languages and styles.
Q4. What does function point analysis estimate?
A. Functionality delivered to users
B. Only physical code lines
C. Only server uptime
D. Only team morale
Answer: A. Functionality delivered to users
Why: Function points estimate functional size based on user-visible capabilities.
Q5. Defect density is commonly calculated as:
A. Tests divided by servers
B. Cost divided by meetings
C. Time divided by users
D. Defects divided by a size measure
Answer: D. Defects divided by a size measure
Why: The denominator may be KLOC, function points, or another defined size unit.
Q6. What does mean time to failure measure?
A. Total requirements
B. Time to write one line
C. Average operating time before failure
D. Number of releases
Answer: C. Average operating time before failure
Why: MTTF estimates the average time a repairable or non-repairable item operates before failure, depending on context.
Q7. What does mean time to repair measure?
A. Average time to restore after a failure
B. Time before the first requirement
C. Average user age
D. Number of code branches
Answer: A. Average time to restore after a failure
Why: MTTR measures restoration or repair duration as defined by the organization.
Q8. Availability is often approximated by:
A. Defects × LOC
B. Effort / features
C. MTTR / MTTF only
D. MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR)
Answer: D. MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR)
Why: For a simple repairable system model, uptime is compared with total uptime plus repair time.
Q9. What is a leading indicator?
A. A historical invoice
B. A measure that may signal future performance or risk
C. A count of final defects only
D. A completed release note
Answer: B. A measure that may signal future performance or risk
Why: Leading indicators can give early warning, though they are not guarantees.
Q10. What is a lagging indicator?
A. A project assumption
B. A measure of outcomes that already occurred
C. A code editor
D. A prediction without data
Answer: B. A measure of outcomes that already occurred
Why: Lagging indicators report past results, such as escaped defects.
Q11. Why define a metric's operational definition?
A. Ensure everyone calculates it consistently
B. Make values impossible to compare
C. Hide data sources
D. Replace interpretation
Answer: A. Ensure everyone calculates it consistently
Why: Clear definitions specify collection rules, units, and boundaries.
Q12. What is measurement validity?
A. Whether the chart is colorful
B. Whether the measure represents the intended concept
C. Whether data looks impressive
D. Whether a team likes it
Answer: B. Whether the measure represents the intended concept
Why: A valid measure reflects the attribute it claims to measure.
Q13. What is measurement reliability?
A. The number of users
B. Consistency when measurement is repeated under similar conditions
C. The number of reports
D. The product's uptime only
Answer: B. Consistency when measurement is repeated under similar conditions
Why: Reliable measurement produces consistent results when conditions are comparable.
Q14. Why can raw LOC be a misleading productivity metric?
A. Languages and coding styles differ in how much work LOC represents
B. LOC directly measures customer value
C. LOC is always impossible to count
D. LOC proves code quality
Answer: A. Languages and coding styles differ in how much work LOC represents
Why: Lines of code do not directly capture complexity, reuse, or delivered value.
Q15. What does cyclomatic complexity estimate?
A. Number of users
B. Total project cost
C. Independent paths through control flow
D. Database size
Answer: C. Independent paths through control flow
Why: Cyclomatic complexity derives from a control-flow graph and relates to path complexity.
Q16. What does code coverage indicate?
A. How much code a test suite executes
B. Whether all requirements are correct
C. Whether no defects exist
D. Whether the UI is attractive
Answer: A. How much code a test suite executes
Why: Coverage is a useful indicator of execution, not a guarantee of correctness.
Q17. What is a KPI?
A. Any number collected without purpose
B. A risk owner
C. A key indicator tied to an important objective
D. A code branch
Answer: C. A key indicator tied to an important objective
Why: KPIs monitor progress toward a defined organizational or project goal.
Q18. Why normalize metrics?
A. Remove units
B. Guarantee better performance
C. Hide all variation
D. Make comparisons fairer across different sizes or contexts
Answer: D. Make comparisons fairer across different sizes or contexts
Why: Normalization can account for scale, such as defects per thousand lines.
Q19. What is a control chart used for?
A. Store source code
B. Design class inheritance
C. Distinguish process variation over time
D. Plan user interviews
Answer: C. Distinguish process variation over time
Why: Control charts help identify unusual variation relative to expected process behavior.
Q20. What is a baseline in measurement?
A. A reference value for comparison
B. A failed build
C. A new user role
D. A random number
Answer: A. A reference value for comparison
Why: A baseline provides context for assessing change or performance.
Q21. Why should metrics be interpreted in context?
A. Numbers explain themselves perfectly
B. Context makes data invalid
C. Numbers can be distorted by scope, complexity, or incentives
D. All teams are identical
Answer: C. Numbers can be distorted by scope, complexity, or incentives
Why: The same metric may mean different things under different conditions.
Q22. What is Goodhart's law warning about?
A. Quality cannot be measured
B. Numbers never affect behavior
C. All metrics are useless
D. A measure can become a poor target when heavily optimized
Answer: D. A measure can become a poor target when heavily optimized
Why: People may game a metric once rewards depend on it, weakening its value.
Q23. Which metric can reflect escaped defects?
A. Story title length
B. Lines formatted per file
C. Defects found by users after release
D. Number of meetings
Answer: C. Defects found by users after release
Why: Escaped defects are found after release, revealing gaps in earlier quality checks.
Q24. What is a defect removal efficiency measure intended to show?
A. Average UI response only
B. Number of developers hired
C. Budget remaining
D. The share of defects found before release compared with total found
Answer: D. The share of defects found before release compared with total found
Why: DRE evaluates how effectively defects are detected before reaching users, based on its defined formula.
Q25. What is a percentile latency measure useful for?
A. Measuring staff turnover
B. Understanding slow responses beyond the average
C. Estimating UI color contrast
D. Counting source files
Answer: B. Understanding slow responses beyond the average
Why: High percentiles such as p95 show response times experienced by slower requests.
Q26. Why use a moving average?
A. Guarantee future results
B. Replace raw data forever
C. Hide all failures permanently
D. Smooth short-term noise to reveal trends
Answer: D. Smooth short-term noise to reveal trends
Why: A moving average helps reveal a trend while individual data points still matter.
Q27. What is a metric gaming risk?
A. Data is stored with units
B. Behavior changes to improve the score rather than the real outcome
C. Results are reviewed
D. Definitions are documented
Answer: B. Behavior changes to improve the score rather than the real outcome
Why: A poorly chosen target can encourage harmful shortcuts or distorted reporting.
Q28. What should be done before comparing two teams' metrics?
A. Assume all teams are identical
B. Ignore data quality
C. Rank only by raw counts
D. Check definitions, context, size, and work type
Answer: D. Check definitions, context, size, and work type
Why: Fair comparison requires comparable definitions and contexts.
Q29. What is a measurement plan?
A. Defines what, why, how, when, and by whom data is collected
B. A customer persona
C. A source-code architecture
D. A deployment package
Answer: A. Defines what, why, how, when, and by whom data is collected
Why: A plan aligns data collection with decisions and responsibilities.
Q30. Why collect metrics tied to decisions?
A. They remove all uncertainty
B. More numbers are always better
C. They help answer a real question and guide action
D. They replace experience
Answer: C. They help answer a real question and guide action
Why: Purpose-driven metrics are more useful than collecting data without a decision need.
Q31. A team compares defects per thousand lines of code across releases. This is an example of:
A. A qualitative opinion
B. A normalized metric
C. A project milestone
D. A risk response
Answer: B. A normalized metric
Why: Normalizing by size supports more meaningful comparisons between releases.
Q32. What is a software metric?
A. A quantitative measure of an attribute
B. A project meeting
C. A design pattern
D. A user role
Answer: A. A quantitative measure of an attribute
Why: Metrics quantify properties of products, processes, or projects.
Q33. What does defect density commonly measure?
A. Defects relative to software size
B. Total staff holidays
C. Number of screens only
D. Project profit only
Answer: A. Defects relative to software size
Why: Defect density relates defects to a size measure such as KLOC or function points.
Q34. Why define a metric clearly?
A. Ensure people interpret it consistently
B. Make results impossible to compare
C. Avoid collecting data
D. Guarantee improvement
Answer: A. Ensure people interpret it consistently
Why: A clear definition supports consistent collection and interpretation.
Q35. What is a leading indicator?
A. A measure that may warn of future problems
B. Only a final outcome measure
C. A code comment
D. A test environment
Answer: A. A measure that may warn of future problems
Why: Leading indicators can signal issues before final results appear.
Q36. What is measurement validation?
A. Checking that a measure represents what it claims to measure
B. Changing numbers to look good
C. Removing units
D. Counting meetings only
Answer: A. Checking that a measure represents what it claims to measure
Why: Valid measures should meaningfully represent the attribute of interest.
Q37. Why avoid comparing teams using raw velocity?
A. Teams may estimate and work differently
B. Velocity is always a security metric
C. It measures memory only
D. All teams have identical context
Answer: A. Teams may estimate and work differently
Why: Velocity depends on team-specific practices and is not a universal comparison.
Q38. What does mean time to repair measure?
A. Average time to restore service after a failure
B. Number of requirements
C. Code line count
D. Time spent in a meeting
Answer: A. Average time to restore service after a failure
Why: MTTR reflects how quickly service is restored after incidents.
Q39. What should happen before acting on a metric?
A. Understand its context and limitations
B. Assume it proves every cause
C. Ignore data quality
D. Use it to rank people automatically
Answer: A. Understand its context and limitations
Why: Metrics need context and should not be treated as complete explanations.
Q40. What does trend analysis of metrics help reveal?
A. Changes in performance or quality over time
B. The exact cause of every defect automatically
C. Only source-code color
D. User passwords
Answer: A. Changes in performance or quality over time
Why: Trends can indicate improvement or emerging problems that need investigation.


14. Software Configuration Management
Q1. What is the main purpose of SCM?
A. Measure user satisfaction
B. Replace testing
C. Write every requirement
D. Control and track changes to software artifacts
Answer: D. Control and track changes to software artifacts
Why: SCM maintains integrity and traceability of changing software items.
Q2. What is a configuration item?
A. An artifact placed under configuration control
B. A random user
C. A server room
D. Any unrecorded chat
Answer: A. An artifact placed under configuration control
Why: Configuration items may include code, requirements, tests, documents, and build scripts.
Q3. What is a baseline in SCM?
A. A developer's memory
B. A defect report
C. An approved reference version controlled through change procedures
D. An unreviewed draft
Answer: C. An approved reference version controlled through change procedures
Why: A baseline provides a stable point for controlled change.
Q4. What does version control record?
A. Only production uptime
B. Only UI screenshots
C. Changes to files over time
D. Only project budget
Answer: C. Changes to files over time
Why: Version control supports history, collaboration, and recovery.
Q5. What is a branch?
A. A final user manual
B. A test oracle
C. A risk score
D. A separate line of development
Answer: D. A separate line of development
Why: Branches isolate work before it is integrated.
Q6. What is a merge conflict?
A. A deployment node
B. A passing build
C. A signed requirement
D. Changes that cannot be combined automatically
Answer: D. Changes that cannot be combined automatically
Why: Conflicting edits need human resolution to preserve intended behavior.
Q7. What is a pull request used for?
A. Replace requirements analysis
B. Delete all version history
C. Propose changes for review before integration
D. Measure response time
Answer: C. Propose changes for review before integration
Why: Pull requests support review, discussion, and controlled merging.
Q8. What is a change control board?
A. A test database
B. A UI widget
C. A compiler
D. A group that evaluates and approves certain changes
Answer: D. A group that evaluates and approves certain changes
Why: A CCB reviews proposed changes according to project governance.
Q9. What is configuration identification?
A. Choosing screen colors
B. Testing only performance
C. Selecting and naming items to be controlled
D. Hiring developers
Answer: C. Selecting and naming items to be controlled
Why: Identification defines what is controlled and how versions are uniquely referenced.
Q10. What is configuration status accounting?
A. Running a load test
B. Recording and reporting item and change status
C. Writing source code
D. Estimating user satisfaction
Answer: B. Recording and reporting item and change status
Why: It tracks versions, approvals, and the state of configuration items.
Q11. What does a configuration audit verify?
A. The product has no users
B. Items match approved records and requirements
C. Every request is fast
D. The project is profitable
Answer: B. Items match approved records and requirements
Why: Audits check completeness and consistency of controlled items and records.
Q12. Why tag a release in version control?
A. Replace build automation
B. Hide changes
C. Identify the exact source state used for a release
D. Delete the baseline
Answer: C. Identify the exact source state used for a release
Why: Tags create a named reference to a specific version.
Q13. What is reproducible build capability?
A. Running only on one developer's laptop
B. Skipping tests
C. Recreating the same build from controlled inputs and environment
D. Changing dependencies silently
Answer: C. Recreating the same build from controlled inputs and environment
Why: Controlled tools, dependencies, and inputs help recreate releases reliably.
Q14. Why pin dependency versions?
A. Reduce unexpected changes from dependency updates
B. Remove the need for testing
C. Prevent all upgrades forever
D. Guarantee no vulnerabilities
Answer: A. Reduce unexpected changes from dependency updates
Why: Pinned versions improve repeatability while still requiring planned updates.
Q15. What is a release branch?
A. A branch for unrelated experiments only
B. A branch used to stabilize a release line
C. A test case
D. A project charter
Answer: B. A branch used to stabilize a release line
Why: Release branches isolate stabilization work from ongoing development.
Q16. What is continuous integration in SCM practice?
A. Integrating changes frequently with automated checks
B. Avoiding shared repositories
C. Merging once at project end
D. Editing production files directly
Answer: A. Integrating changes frequently with automated checks
Why: Frequent integration reduces long-lived divergence and reveals problems early.
Q17. What should accompany an approved change?
A. A deleted test plan
B. No review
C. Impact assessment and traceable records
D. An unrecorded direct edit
Answer: C. Impact assessment and traceable records
Why: Traceable change records explain what changed, why, and who approved it.
Q18. Why separate source from build artifacts?
A. Hide release versions
B. Make builds impossible
C. Avoid mixing generated outputs with editable source history
D. Remove automation
Answer: C. Avoid mixing generated outputs with editable source history
Why: Generated files can be recreated and may clutter or confuse source changes.
Q19. What is semantic versioning commonly used to communicate?
A. Test coverage only
B. Compatibility significance of releases
C. Number of employees
D. Project budget
Answer: B. Compatibility significance of releases
Why: Major, minor, and patch numbers signal types of change under a defined scheme.
Q20. What is a hotfix branch for?
A. Replace the main branch forever
B. Track stakeholder interviews
C. Store only UI sketches
D. Isolate an urgent production fix
Answer: D. Isolate an urgent production fix
Why: A hotfix branch allows focused urgent work with controlled integration.
Q21. Why review merge changes?
A. Avoid accountability
B. Replace tests completely
C. Guarantee all future changes are safe
D. Catch defects and unintended edits before integration
Answer: D. Catch defects and unintended edits before integration
Why: Review provides another check on correctness, security, and maintainability.
Q22. What is configuration drift?
A. Two developers share code
B. Actual environments diverge from approved configuration
C. A release is tagged
D. A test passes
Answer: B. Actual environments diverge from approved configuration
Why: Drift creates differences that can cause inconsistent behavior between environments.
Q23. What is infrastructure as code useful for?
A. Measuring defect density
B. Writing user stories
C. Versioning and repeatably applying environment configuration
D. Replacing all application code
Answer: C. Versioning and repeatably applying environment configuration
Why: Infrastructure definitions can be reviewed, versioned, and recreated.
Q24. Why keep release notes?
A. Communicate changes, fixes, and known issues
B. Guarantee no support calls
C. Hide breaking changes
D. Replace test results
Answer: A. Communicate changes, fixes, and known issues
Why: Release notes help users and operators understand the release.
Q25. What is a merge strategy?
A. A defined way to integrate changes from branches
B. A usability heuristic
C. A requirements interview
D. A project risk score
Answer: A. A defined way to integrate changes from branches
Why: Strategies such as merge commits or rebasing affect history and integration workflow.
Q26. What is artifact provenance?
A. A sprint goal
B. The UI's color scheme
C. A user password
D. Evidence of where an artifact came from and how it was produced
Answer: D. Evidence of where an artifact came from and how it was produced
Why: Provenance supports trust, auditing, and supply-chain security.
Q27. Why protect the main branch?
A. Make collaboration impossible
B. Stop all releases
C. Avoid tests
D. Prevent unreviewed or failing changes from entering stable code
Answer: D. Prevent unreviewed or failing changes from entering stable code
Why: Branch protections can require reviews and successful checks.
Q28. What is a rollback in release management?
A. Return to a known prior version after a failed release
B. Merge every branch
C. Approve a new requirement
D. Delete test evidence
Answer: A. Return to a known prior version after a failed release
Why: Rollback restores a prior version or configuration to reduce impact.
Q29. What does a software bill of materials list?
A. Components and dependencies included in a product
B. Employee salaries
C. Only test cases
D. UI pages
Answer: A. Components and dependencies included in a product
Why: An SBOM helps identify included components and assess supply-chain exposure.
Q30. What is the purpose of an SCM plan?
A. Replace source control
B. Define roles, tools, identification, change, and audit procedures
C. Specify only screen layouts
D. Guarantee no conflicts
Answer: B. Define roles, tools, identification, change, and audit procedures
Why: An SCM plan sets the rules for controlling and tracking product changes.
Q31. Why is a baseline useful in configuration management?
A. It removes the need for approvals
B. It identifies an agreed version controlled against changes
C. It prevents all defects
D. It replaces backups
Answer: B. It identifies an agreed version controlled against changes
Why: A baseline is an approved reference point for controlled change.
Q32. What is a configuration item?
A. An artifact managed under configuration control
B. A random chat message
C. A staff lunch order
D. A user opinion only
Answer: A. An artifact managed under configuration control
Why: Configuration items are selected artifacts tracked and controlled.
Q33. What is a version baseline?
A. An approved snapshot of configuration items
B. A temporary password
C. An unreviewed idea
D. A test failure
Answer: A. An approved snapshot of configuration items
Why: A baseline provides a controlled reference for changes.
Q34. Why use version control?
A. Track history and coordinate changes
B. Replace all testing
C. Guarantee correct requirements
D. Hide code changes
Answer: A. Track history and coordinate changes
Why: Version control supports history, branching, and collaboration.
Q35. What is change control?
A. Assessing and authorizing changes systematically
B. Applying all changes secretly
C. Deleting baselines
D. Avoiding impact analysis
Answer: A. Assessing and authorizing changes systematically
Why: Change control evaluates impact and records decisions.
Q36. What is a configuration audit?
A. Checking that items match records and requirements
B. Writing a user story
C. Running a brainstorm
D. Estimating team morale
Answer: A. Checking that items match records and requirements
Why: Audits verify consistency and correctness of configuration records.
Q37. What does a release tag help identify?
A. A specific version of source or artifacts
B. A user interface color
C. A staff role
D. A budget category
Answer: A. A specific version of source or artifacts
Why: Tags mark a particular version for reference or release.
Q38. Why create reproducible builds?
A. Allow the same source and settings to produce consistent outputs
B. Avoid recording dependencies
C. Make versions ambiguous
D. Remove deployment checks
Answer: A. Allow the same source and settings to produce consistent outputs
Why: Reproducibility supports reliable builds and investigations.
Q39. What is configuration status accounting?
A. Recording and reporting item versions and change status
B. Counting office supplies
C. Testing usability only
D. Writing requirements
Answer: A. Recording and reporting item versions and change status
Why: Status accounting tracks configuration identity, history, and state.
Q40. What is branching used for in version control?
A. Develop changes separately before integration
B. Delete all history
C. Replace testing
D. Approve project budgets
Answer: A. Develop changes separately before integration
Why: Branches isolate work until it is ready to be integrated.


15. Software Risk Management
Q1. A risk is best described as:
A. An uncertain event that may affect objectives
B. A completed task
C. A defect that has definitely occurred
D. A guaranteed benefit
Answer: A. An uncertain event that may affect objectives
Why: Risk involves uncertainty and possible effects on project or product objectives.
Q2. What is risk identification?
A. Counting code lines
B. Closing a release
C. Fixing a known bug only
D. Finding and describing potential risks
Answer: D. Finding and describing potential risks
Why: Identification records possible events, causes, and effects.
Q3. Risk probability describes:
A. Cost after the event only
B. How long code is
C. Likelihood that the event will occur
D. Number of developers
Answer: C. Likelihood that the event will occur
Why: Probability estimates how likely the risk is within a defined period or context.
Q4. Risk impact describes:
A. The number of test files
B. A team's velocity
C. Consequences if the risk occurs
D. The branch name
Answer: C. Consequences if the risk occurs
Why: Impact estimates the effect on cost, schedule, quality, security, or business goals.
Q5. A common qualitative risk score uses:
A. Tests and meetings only
B. Lines of code and colors
C. Probability and impact
D. Users and screens only
Answer: C. Probability and impact
Why: A probability-impact matrix helps prioritize risks consistently.
Q6. What is risk mitigation?
A. Recording no owner
B. Accepting every outcome without thought
C. Pretending the risk is gone
D. Reducing likelihood or impact
Answer: D. Reducing likelihood or impact
Why: Mitigation takes action to lower exposure before the risk occurs.
Q7. What is risk avoidance?
A. Waiting for failure
B. Changing the plan to remove the threat or exposure
C. Transferring insurance only
D. Ignoring the risk
Answer: B. Changing the plan to remove the threat or exposure
Why: Avoidance changes the approach so the risk no longer applies or is eliminated.
Q8. What is risk transfer?
A. Deleting the risk register
B. Making probability zero
C. Shifting some financial or operational impact to another party
D. Testing every line
Answer: C. Shifting some financial or operational impact to another party
Why: Contracts or insurance can transfer certain consequences, but not all responsibility.
Q9. What is risk acceptance?
A. Avoiding documentation
B. Failing to notice a risk
C. Guaranteeing success
D. Consciously retaining a risk, often with a contingency
Answer: D. Consciously retaining a risk, often with a contingency
Why: Acceptance is a deliberate decision based on exposure and response cost.
Q10. What is a contingency plan?
A. A list of completed features
B. A UI mock-up
C. Planned action if a risk occurs
D. A coding convention
Answer: C. Planned action if a risk occurs
Why: Contingency plans define responses to a realized risk or trigger.
Q11. Who is a risk owner?
A. Only the customer
B. Person accountable for monitoring and managing a risk
C. The software compiler
D. Anyone who sees the project
Answer: B. Person accountable for monitoring and managing a risk
Why: A named owner tracks the risk and coordinates responses.
Q12. What is a risk trigger?
A. A source-code comment
B. A final invoice
C. A test passed
D. A warning sign that a risk may be occurring
Answer: D. A warning sign that a risk may be occurring
Why: Triggers indicate when planned response actions may be needed.
Q13. What is residual risk?
A. Risk remaining after responses are applied
B. A closed task
C. A risk that is impossible
D. A risk never identified
Answer: A. Risk remaining after responses are applied
Why: Mitigation often reduces exposure but does not remove it completely.
Q14. What is secondary risk?
A. A new risk caused by a risk response
B. A user requirement
C. A completed defect
D. The original risk score
Answer: A. A new risk caused by a risk response
Why: Responses can introduce new issues that should also be assessed.
Q15. Which risk is most urgent?
A. Low probability and negligible impact
B. High probability and high impact
C. A closed risk
D. No uncertainty and no impact
Answer: B. High probability and high impact
Why: High exposure generally deserves prompt attention and response planning.
Q16. Why review risks throughout a project?
A. Only final risks matter
B. Risk is fixed after kickoff
C. Conditions and exposure change over time
D. Reviews eliminate all uncertainty
Answer: C. Conditions and exposure change over time
Why: New information can change likelihood, impact, and response priorities.
Q17. What is a risk register?
A. A staff roster
B. A record of risks, owners, ratings, and responses
C. A code repository
D. A test report only
Answer: B. A record of risks, owners, ratings, and responses
Why: It provides a shared place to track risk information and actions.
Q18. What is schedule risk?
A. A UI defect only
B. A data type
C. A test oracle
D. Uncertainty that may delay planned milestones
Answer: D. Uncertainty that may delay planned milestones
Why: Dependencies, estimates, and resource constraints can threaten dates.
Q19. What is technical risk?
A. Only meeting time
B. Only staff attendance
C. Only market advertising
D. Uncertainty about technology, integration, or performance
Answer: D. Uncertainty about technology, integration, or performance
Why: Technical uncertainty can affect feasibility, quality, and delivery.
Q20. What is a risk appetite?
A. A testing tool
B. A software feature
C. The number of risks in a list
D. The amount and type of risk an organization is willing to accept
Answer: D. The amount and type of risk an organization is willing to accept
Why: Risk appetite guides decisions about acceptable exposure.
Q21. What is a risk threshold?
A. A code style rule
B. A release name
C. A class method
D. A level of exposure that triggers action or escalation
Answer: D. A level of exposure that triggers action or escalation
Why: Thresholds make escalation and response decisions more consistent.
Q22. Why estimate risk exposure?
A. Help compare and prioritize risks
B. Replace monitoring
C. Prove outcomes are certain
D. Guarantee budgets
Answer: A. Help compare and prioritize risks
Why: Exposure combines likelihood and consequence to support prioritization.
Q23. What is opportunity risk management concerned with?
A. Only harmful threats
B. Only coding defects
C. Uncertain events that may create beneficial outcomes
D. Only test coverage
Answer: C. Uncertain events that may create beneficial outcomes
Why: Opportunities can be exploited, enhanced, shared, or accepted.
Q24. A key supplier may fail. What response helps reduce dependence?
A. Qualify an alternative supplier
B. Hide the contract
C. Ignore delivery dates
D. Remove all monitoring
Answer: A. Qualify an alternative supplier
Why: An alternative supplier can reduce exposure to a single point of dependency.
Q25. A new framework is unproven. What is a useful early response?
A. Adopt it everywhere immediately
B. Assume it will work
C. Skip integration tests
D. Run a focused technical proof of concept
Answer: D. Run a focused technical proof of concept
Why: A proof of concept reduces uncertainty before broad commitment.
Q26. What is risk escalation?
A. Transfer it to a tester without agreement
B. Delete the risk
C. Refer a risk to the level able to make the needed decision
D. Wait until project end
Answer: C. Refer a risk to the level able to make the needed decision
Why: Escalation is appropriate when authority or impact exceeds the team's remit.
Q27. What is a risk burndown chart used to show?
A. Risk exposure changing over time
B. Only source-code lines
C. UI navigation
D. Only staff hours
Answer: A. Risk exposure changing over time
Why: It visualizes whether overall tracked risk exposure is decreasing or increasing.
Q28. Why document assumptions as risks?
A. An assumption may prove false and disrupt plans
B. Assumptions can never fail
C. It removes the need for estimates
D. Documentation causes all risks
Answer: A. An assumption may prove false and disrupt plans
Why: Unverified assumptions create uncertainty that may need monitoring.
Q29. What is risk response effectiveness?
A. Whether a plan has a long title
B. Whether actions actually reduce exposure as intended
C. How many meetings occurred
D. Whether all risks are hidden
Answer: B. Whether actions actually reduce exposure as intended
Why: Teams should check outcomes and adapt ineffective responses.
Q30. What should happen when a risk becomes an issue?
A. Remove all records
B. Wait without action
C. Execute the response and manage the realized problem
D. Keep it only as a hypothetical risk
Answer: C. Execute the response and manage the realized problem
Why: Once realized, it requires issue management as well as any continuing risk tracking.
Q31. A risk is unlikely but would stop a critical service if it occurs. What should guide its priority?
A. Probability alone
B. Impact and likelihood together
C. The date it was reported only
D. The name of its owner
Answer: B. Impact and likelihood together
Why: Risk priority considers both likelihood and potential impact.
Q32. What is a software risk?
A. An uncertain event that may affect objectives
B. A confirmed feature
C. A coding standard
D. A completed milestone
Answer: A. An uncertain event that may affect objectives
Why: Risk involves uncertainty and possible impact on objectives.
Q33. How is risk exposure often estimated?
A. Probability multiplied by impact
B. Lines of code plus screens
C. Number of meetings
D. Cost minus schedule
Answer: A. Probability multiplied by impact
Why: A simple risk score combines likelihood and consequence.
Q34. What is risk mitigation?
A. Taking steps to reduce likelihood or impact
B. Ignoring a threat
C. Recording only success
D. Guaranteeing no uncertainty
Answer: A. Taking steps to reduce likelihood or impact
Why: Mitigation reduces the chance or consequences of a risk.
Q35. What is a contingency plan?
A. A planned response if a risk occurs
B. A list of completed tasks
C. A coding style guide
D. A product logo
Answer: A. A planned response if a risk occurs
Why: Contingency plans describe actions to take if an event happens.
Q36. Who should own a project risk?
A. A person responsible for monitoring and response
B. No one
C. Only the end user always
D. The compiler
Answer: A. A person responsible for monitoring and response
Why: A named owner helps ensure the risk is monitored and managed.
Q37. What is risk avoidance?
A. Changing the plan to eliminate a particular exposure
B. Accepting all risks blindly
C. Measuring code coverage
D. Ignoring warning signs
Answer: A. Changing the plan to eliminate a particular exposure
Why: Avoidance changes the approach so the threat no longer applies.
Q38. When should risks be reviewed?
A. Throughout the project
B. Only after the product retires
C. Never after planning
D. Only when all work is done
Answer: A. Throughout the project
Why: Risks change as the project progresses and need ongoing review.
Q39. What is residual risk?
A. Risk remaining after a response
B. A risk that was never identified
C. A completed test
D. A fixed requirement
Answer: A. Risk remaining after a response
Why: Responses may reduce risk without removing it completely.
Q40. What is risk acceptance?
A. Acknowledging a risk and choosing not to take further action for now
B. Removing all uncertainty
C. Hiding the risk
D. Automatically cancelling the project
Answer: A. Acknowledging a risk and choosing not to take further action for now
Why: A team may accept a risk when its exposure is tolerable or response costs outweigh benefits.


16. Software Security Engineering
Q1. What is the principle of least privilege?
A. Give all users administrator rights
B. Share one account
C. Give each identity only the access it needs
D. Disable access logs
Answer: C. Give each identity only the access it needs
Why: Limiting permissions reduces the damage from mistakes or compromised accounts.
Q2. What is authentication?
A. Encrypting a backup
B. Checking UI layout
C. Deciding what it may access
D. Verifying who an entity is
Answer: D. Verifying who an entity is
Why: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permitted actions.
Q3. What is authorization?
A. Proving identity only
B. Finding syntax errors
C. Hashing a password
D. Determining permitted actions after identity is established
Answer: D. Determining permitted actions after identity is established
Why: Authorization applies access rules to resources and actions.
Q4. Why store password hashes rather than plaintext passwords?
A. Hashes are reversible by design
B. It removes the need for TLS
C. A database leak should not directly reveal original passwords
D. It prevents phishing
Answer: C. A database leak should not directly reveal original passwords
Why: A slow, salted password-hashing scheme makes stolen password databases harder to exploit.
Q5. What is a salt in password storage?
A. An encryption key shared by all users
B. A user's recovery email
C. A unique random value added before hashing
D. A session cookie
Answer: C. A unique random value added before hashing
Why: Unique salts prevent identical passwords from producing identical stored hashes and hinder precomputed attacks.
Q6. What does SQL injection exploit?
A. Weak UI contrast
B. A slow CPU
C. Untrusted input treated as part of a SQL command
D. A missing project plan
Answer: C. Untrusted input treated as part of a SQL command
Why: Unsafe query construction lets input alter database command structure.
Q7. What is the preferred defense against SQL injection?
A. Using longer passwords only
B. Hiding error messages only
C. String concatenation
D. Parameterized queries
Answer: D. Parameterized queries
Why: Parameters separate data from query syntax.
Q8. What is cross-site scripting (XSS)?
A. Attacker-controlled script runs in a user's browser
B. A network routing issue
C. A database backup failure
D. A project scheduling risk
Answer: A. Attacker-controlled script runs in a user's browser
Why: XSS occurs when untrusted content is executed as script in a browser context.
Q9. What helps prevent XSS?
A. Trusting all input
B. Context-aware output encoding and safe templating
C. Storing passwords in plain text
D. Disabling all logs
