C. Number of pointers in a graph
D. Number of stored elements
Correct answer: D. Number of stored elements
Explanation: Size is the count of actual elements, while capacity is allocated storage.
37. In a dynamic array, capacity means:
A. The largest element value
B. Number of elements that can fit before resizing
C. Number of currently occupied elements only
D. The number of array dimensions
Correct answer: B. Number of elements that can fit before resizing
Explanation: Capacity describes allocated room, which may exceed the current size.
38. A sparse representation is useful when:
A. Every position must contain a different value
B. There are exactly two elements
C. Most possible positions contain no meaningful value
D. Data is always sorted
Correct answer: C. Most possible positions contain no meaningful value
Explanation: Sparse representations can save space when most entries are empty or zero.
39. After deleting a node from a singly linked list, the predecessor should generally:
A. Point to the deleted node's successor
B. Be converted into an array
C. Lose all its data
D. Point to itself always
Correct answer: A. Point to the deleted node's successor
Explanation: Updating the predecessor link bypasses the removed node.
40. An empty linked list commonly has its head set to:
A. A required dummy value only
B. The number one
C. The last array index
D. Null / no node
Correct answer: D. Null / no node
Explanation: A null head is a common representation of an empty list.
41. If A, then B, then C are pushed onto an empty stack, the first popped item is:
A. B
B. C
C. A
D. No item
Correct answer: B. C
Explanation: LIFO means the last pushed item, C, is removed first.
42. If A, then B, then C are enqueued into an empty queue, the first dequeued item is:
A. A
B. No item
C. B
D. C
Correct answer: A. A
Explanation: FIFO means the first enqueued item, A, leaves first.
43. The front of a queue identifies the:
A. Last array position always
B. Largest item
C. Next item to be removed
D. Next item to be inserted only
Correct answer: C. Next item to be removed
Explanation: The front points to the next item due for dequeue.
44. The rear of a queue identifies the:
A. Smallest priority
B. End where new items are inserted
C. Next item to be removed
D. Head of a tree
Correct answer: B. End where new items are inserted
Explanation: Enqueue typically adds an item at the rear.
45. Linked-list nodes are commonly allocated:
A. Only in one fixed contiguous block
B. At the same address
C. Only on a disk
D. Dynamically and need not be adjacent in memory
Correct answer: D. Dynamically and need not be adjacent in memory
Explanation: Nodes may occupy different memory locations connected by pointers.
46. A stack can be implemented using:
A. Only a binary tree
B. Only a graph
C. Only a sorting algorithm
D. An array or a linked list
Correct answer: D. An array or a linked list
Explanation: Both arrays and linked lists can support stack operations.
47. A queue can be implemented using:
A. Only a hash function
B. Only a recursion formula
C. Only a binary search tree
D. An array or a linked list
Correct answer: D. An array or a linked list
Explanation: Either representation can maintain front and rear operations.
48. A typical singly linked-list traversal stops when:
A. The current pointer becomes null
B. The node has two children
C. The data equals zero in every case
D. The pointer reaches index -1
Correct answer: A. The current pointer becomes null
Explanation: Null indicates there is no next node in a standard non-circular list.
49. Why is binary search generally unsuitable for a basic linked list?
A. Binary search requires a queue
B. The middle element cannot be reached efficiently by index
C. Linked lists cannot hold sorted data
D. Lists never contain numbers
Correct answer: B. The middle element cannot be reached efficiently by index
Explanation: Repeatedly finding the middle node takes traversal, removing binary search's usual advantage.
50. Which queue operation pair is most standard?
A. Hash and rehash
B. Left rotation and right rotation
C. Enqueue and dequeue
D. Push and pop
Correct answer: C. Enqueue and dequeue
Explanation: Enqueue inserts; dequeue removes from the front.


3. Non-Linear Data Structures
Choose the best answer. The correct option and a brief explanation follow each question.
1. Which data structure represents hierarchical relationships?
A. Stack
B. Queue
C. One-dimensional array
D. Tree
Correct answer: D. Tree
Explanation: A tree contains nodes arranged in parent-child relationships.
2. The root of a tree is the node that:
A. Has exactly two parents
B. Has no children always
C. Must be the smallest value
D. Has no parent
Correct answer: D. Has no parent
Explanation: The root is the topmost node and has no parent.
3. A leaf node is a node that:
A. Must have two children
B. Has no parent
C. Has no children
D. Is always the root
Correct answer: C. Has no children
Explanation: Leaves are terminal nodes in a tree.
4. In a tree, an edge connects:
A. Two arrays only
B. Two nodes
C. A key to a hash function only
D. A queue to a stack
Correct answer: B. Two nodes
Explanation: Edges represent links between nodes.
5. A binary tree node can have at most:
A. One child
B. Two children
C. Any fixed number of five
D. Three children
Correct answer: B. Two children
Explanation: Binary trees limit each node to left and right child positions.
6. In a full binary tree, each node has:
A. No parent and no child
B. Exactly one child
C. At least three children
D. Either zero or two children
Correct answer: D. Either zero or two children
Explanation: A full binary tree has no node with exactly one child.
7. A complete binary tree has levels filled:
A. Fully except possibly the last, which fills from left to right
B. With leaves at the root
C. In random order only
D. Only on the right side
Correct answer: A. Fully except possibly the last, which fills from left to right
Explanation: Completeness packs nodes level by level from the left.
8. In a perfect binary tree, all internal nodes have two children and:
A. There are no internal nodes
B. Every node has one child
C. The root is a leaf in all cases
D. All leaves are at the same depth
Correct answer: D. All leaves are at the same depth
Explanation: Perfect trees have fully filled levels and equal leaf depth.
9. In a BST, values in the left subtree are typically:
A. Always greater than the node's key
B. Less than the node's key
C. Stored only in leaves
D. All equal to the root
Correct answer: B. Less than the node's key
Explanation: The BST ordering property places smaller keys left and larger keys right, subject to duplicate policy.
10. Searching a balanced BST takes typically:
A. O(n²)
B. O(2ⁿ)
C. O(log n)
D. O(1) for every key
Correct answer: C. O(log n)
Explanation: A balanced tree reduces the search region by roughly half at each level.
11. A highly skewed BST can have search time:
A. O(1/n)
B. Always O(log n)
C. O(n)
D. Always O(1)
Correct answer: C. O(n)
Explanation: A skewed tree can behave like a linked list.
12. Which is the preorder traversal order?
A. Left, root, right
B. Right, left, root
C. Root, left, right
D. Left, right, root
Correct answer: C. Root, left, right
Explanation: Preorder visits the root before its subtrees.
13. Which is the inorder traversal order?
A. Root, right, left
B. Left, root, right
C. Root, left, right
D. Left, right, root
Correct answer: B. Left, root, right
Explanation: Inorder visits left subtree, node, then right subtree.
14. Which is the postorder traversal order?
A. Root, right, left
B. Left, root, right
C. Root, left, right
D. Left, right, root
Correct answer: D. Left, right, root
Explanation: Postorder visits children before the root.
15. Level-order traversal commonly uses a:
A. Queue
B. Sorting network
C. Hash function
D. Stack only
Correct answer: A. Queue
Explanation: A queue processes nodes in breadth-first order.
16. Depth-first search commonly uses recursion or a:
A. Hash key only
B. Queue only
C. Heap array only
D. Stack
Correct answer: D. Stack
Explanation: DFS explores deeply before backtracking, often using a stack.
17. Breadth-first search explores nodes:
A. From leaf to root only
B. Level by level
C. In sorted order always
D. Only by descending key value
Correct answer: B. Level by level
Explanation: BFS visits all reachable neighbors at the current distance before going deeper.
18. A graph consists of:
A. Only array indices
B. A single stack
C. Only parent and child fields
D. Vertices and edges
Correct answer: D. Vertices and edges
Explanation: Vertices represent entities and edges represent relationships.
19. In a directed graph, an edge has:
A. No endpoints
B. Both directions by definition
C. A specified direction
D. A weight but no vertices
Correct answer: C. A specified direction
Explanation: A directed edge goes from one vertex to another in a specified direction.
20. In an undirected graph, an edge:
A. Can only point upward
B. Must be a loop
C. Has no direction
D. Always has a negative weight
Correct answer: C. Has no direction
Explanation: An undirected edge represents a two-way relationship.
21. A weighted graph assigns:
A. A sorted index to all nodes
B. A stack to every edge
C. A value or cost to edges (or sometimes vertices)
D. A parent to every vertex
Correct answer: C. A value or cost to edges (or sometimes vertices)
Explanation: Weights can represent distance, cost, time, or another measure.
22. An adjacency matrix represents graph connections using:
A. A linked stack only
B. A single scalar
C. A two-dimensional table
D. A recursive call list
Correct answer: C. A two-dimensional table
Explanation: Matrix entries indicate whether edges exist and may store weights.
23. An adjacency list stores:
A. Only a matrix diagonal
B. A sorted tree for each array index always
C. A list of neighbors for each vertex
D. Only one global edge
Correct answer: C. A list of neighbors for each vertex
Explanation: Adjacency lists are often memory-efficient for sparse graphs.
24. A sparse graph has relatively:
A. Every possible edge
B. Exactly one edge per vertex
C. Few edges compared with the possible number
D. No vertices
Correct answer: C. Few edges compared with the possible number
Explanation: Sparse graphs have far fewer than the maximum possible edges.
25. A dense graph has:
A. Only one vertex
B. Only directed self-loops
C. No edges
D. Many edges relative to the number of possible edges
Correct answer: D. Many edges relative to the number of possible edges
Explanation: Dense graphs contain a high proportion of possible connections.
26. A cycle is a path that:
A. Can only occur in an array
B. Always has one vertex and no edge
C. Must contain no edges
D. Returns to its starting vertex without repeating edges/vertices internally under the usual simple-cycle definition
Correct answer: D. Returns to its starting vertex without repeating edges/vertices internally under the usual simple-cycle definition
Explanation: A cycle returns to its start; definitions of simple cycles restrict repeated internal vertices.
27. An undirected graph is connected if:
A. Every pair of vertices has a path between them
B. All edge weights are equal
C. Every vertex has degree zero
D. It has no edges
Correct answer: A. Every pair of vertices has a path between them
Explanation: Connectivity means all vertices are mutually reachable by paths.
28. In an undirected graph, the degree of a vertex is the:
A. Weight of the smallest edge
B. Length of a path to the root
C. Number of trees in memory
D. Number of incident edges
Correct answer: D. Number of incident edges
Explanation: Degree counts edges touching a vertex, with loops treated according to convention.
29. A path in a graph is:
A. A hash bucket only
B. A sequence of vertices connected by edges
C. A sorting comparison
D. A single memory address
Correct answer: B. A sequence of vertices connected by edges
Explanation: A path describes a route through connected vertices.
30. Dijkstra's algorithm is used for shortest paths with:
A. Unweighted strings only
B. No edges
C. Only negative edge weights
D. Non-negative edge weights
Correct answer: D. Non-negative edge weights
Explanation: Dijkstra's standard algorithm assumes non-negative edge weights.
31. In an unweighted graph, BFS can find:
A. A sorted vertex list
B. Only a cycle
C. A shortest path in number of edges
D. A maximum-weight spanning tree always
Correct answer: C. A shortest path in number of edges
Explanation: BFS explores by distance layers, so first discovery gives a shortest edge-count path.
32. DFS can be used to detect:
A. Cycles and connected components (with suitable handling)
B. Only array capacity
C. Only the median of numbers
D. Only queue overflow
Correct answer: A. Cycles and connected components (with suitable handling)
Explanation: DFS explores graph structure and supports cycle detection and component discovery.
33. A spanning tree of a connected undirected graph:
A. Has no path between vertices
B. Contains only one vertex always
C. Connects all vertices without cycles
D. Must contain every possible edge
Correct answer: C. Connects all vertices without cycles
Explanation: A spanning tree includes all vertices and has no cycles.
34. A minimum spanning tree minimizes:
A. Every individual edge independently
B. The total weight of its selected edges
C. The number of vertices to zero
D. The graph's number of possible paths
Correct answer: B. The total weight of its selected edges
Explanation: An MST connects all vertices with minimum total edge weight.
35. Kruskal's algorithm builds an MST by:
A. Adding light edges that do not create a cycle
B. Sorting vertices by name only
C. Always choosing the heaviest edge first
D. Visiting only leaves
Correct answer: A. Adding light edges that do not create a cycle
Explanation: Kruskal considers edges in increasing weight and avoids cycles.
36. Prim's algorithm grows an MST by:
A. Using only depth-first traversal
B. Deleting the smallest vertex
C. Reversing every edge
D. Expanding one tree using a minimum connecting edge
Correct answer: D. Expanding one tree using a minimum connecting edge
Explanation: Prim repeatedly adds the lowest-weight edge connecting the current tree to a new vertex.
37. A binary heap is commonly used to implement a:
A. Priority queue
B. Doubly linked list only
C. Graph adjacency matrix only
D. Simple text file
Correct answer: A. Priority queue
Explanation: A heap efficiently exposes the minimum or maximum priority element.
38. In a max heap, each parent key is:
A. Always equal to both children
B. Unrelated to child keys
C. Smaller than every child
D. At least as large as its children's keys
Correct answer: D. At least as large as its children's keys
Explanation: The max-heap property places the largest key at the root.
39. In a min heap, the root contains:
A. A minimum key
B. The newest inserted key always
C. A random leaf
D. The maximum key always
Correct answer: A. A minimum key
Explanation: The min-heap property makes the smallest key available at the root.
40. A binary heap is usually a:
A. Perfectly skewed tree
B. Complete binary tree
C. Circular linked list
D. Graph with no vertices
Correct answer: B. Complete binary tree
Explanation: The complete shape supports compact array representation.
41. In a zero-based heap array, the left child of index i is at:
A. 2i + 1
B. 2i + 2 only
C. i/2
D. 2i
Correct answer: A. 2i + 1
Explanation: For zero-based indexing, left and right child indices are 2i+1 and 2i+2.
42. An AVL tree is a:
A. Hashing method
B. Queue with priorities
C. Graph with negative edges
D. Self-balancing binary search tree
Correct answer: D. Self-balancing binary search tree
Explanation: AVL trees maintain a balance condition using rotations.
43. Why are rotations used in AVL trees?
A. To restore balance while preserving BST order
B. To reverse every key
C. To turn the tree into a queue
D. To remove all leaves
Correct answer: A. To restore balance while preserving BST order
Explanation: Rotations restructure links locally without violating search-tree ordering.
44. A trie is especially useful for:
A. Prefix-based string lookup
B. Implementing a circular queue
C. Storing edge weights only
D. Scheduling CPU processes only
Correct answer: A. Prefix-based string lookup
Explanation: Tries organize strings by shared prefixes.
45. B-trees are commonly used in:
A. Only graphics colors
B. Databases and file systems
C. Only recursive arithmetic
D. Only stack evaluation
Correct answer: B. Databases and file systems
Explanation: B-trees keep data balanced and reduce disk access for large indexes.
46. The height of a tree is commonly measured by the:
A. Number of queues in memory
B. Sum of all key values
C. Longest path from root to a leaf, in edges or levels by convention
D. Number of keys in the root
Correct answer: C. Longest path from root to a leaf, in edges or levels by convention
Explanation: Height measures the maximum depth; conventions differ on counting edges versus nodes.
47. A tree is a connected acyclic:
A. Graph
B. Array
C. Hash function
D. Stack
Correct answer: A. Graph
Explanation: A tree is a special graph with connectivity and no cycles.
48. A topological ordering exists for a:
A. Single stack
B. Graph with a directed cycle
C. Undirected complete graph only
D. Directed acyclic graph (DAG)
Correct answer: D. Directed acyclic graph (DAG)
Explanation: A DAG can order vertices so every directed edge goes forward in the order.
49. In a directed graph, indegree counts:
A. All vertices in the graph
B. The weight of a path
C. Edges entering a vertex
D. Edges leaving a vertex only
Correct answer: C. Edges entering a vertex
Explanation: Indegree counts incoming directed edges.
50. In a directed graph, outdegree counts:
A. The number of leaves in a tree
B. Edges leaving a vertex
C. The number of array positions
D. Edges entering a vertex only
Correct answer: B. Edges leaving a vertex
Explanation: Outdegree counts outgoing directed edges.


4. Searching Algorithms
Choose the best answer. The correct option and a brief explanation follow each question.
1. Linear search finds a target by:
A. Using a hash function only
B. Building a tree first
C. Halving the search range each time
D. Checking elements one by one
Correct answer: D. Checking elements one by one
Explanation: Linear search examines items sequentially until a match or the end.
2. Worst-case time for linear search in n items is:
A. O(1)
B. O(n log n)
C. O(log n)
D. O(n)
Correct answer: D. O(n)
Explanation: The target may be last or absent, requiring all n items to be checked.
3. The best case for linear search occurs when the target is:
A. Always duplicated
B. Absent from the list
C. At the first position
D. At the last position only
Correct answer: C. At the first position
Explanation: A first-position match requires only one comparison.
4. Binary search requires the data to be:
A. All identical
B. Stored only in a queue
C. Stored only in a graph
D. Sorted by the searched key
Correct answer: D. Sorted by the searched key
Explanation: Binary search uses ordering to discard half the search interval.
5. What does binary search compare first in a range?
A. The target with every element
B. The target with a random edge
C. The target with the last element only
D. The target with the middle element
Correct answer: D. The target with the middle element
Explanation: The middle comparison determines which half can still contain the target.
6. Binary search on a sorted array has worst-case time:
A. O(2ⁿ)
B. O(log n)
C. O(n)
D. O(n²)
Correct answer: B. O(log n)
Explanation: Each comparison approximately halves the remaining range.
7. If the target is smaller than the middle key in ascending-order binary search, search:
A. The whole list from the start
B. Only the last element
C. The left half
D. The right half
Correct answer: C. The left half
Explanation: Smaller values can only occur before the middle in ascending order.
8. If the target is larger than the middle key in ascending-order binary search, search:
A. The right half
B. No half; stop immediately
C. The left half
D. Only the first element
Correct answer: A. The right half
Explanation: Larger values can only occur after the middle in ascending order.
9. A common safe midpoint formula in code is:
A. high - low + high
B. (low + high) * high
C. low * high * 2
D. low + (high - low) // 2
Correct answer: D. low + (high - low) // 2
Explanation: This form avoids potential overflow in fixed-width integer languages.
10. An iterative binary search typically updates:
A. Every value in the array
B. The queue's priority
C. Low and high boundaries
D. Only a graph's indegree
Correct answer: C. Low and high boundaries
Explanation: The search interval shrinks by changing its low or high boundary.
11. A recursive binary search needs a base case for:
A. A queue to become full
B. Every array to be reversed
C. A match or an empty search interval
D. Every value to be hashed
Correct answer: C. A match or an empty search interval
Explanation: The recursion stops when it finds the key or no valid interval remains.
12. With duplicate keys, ordinary binary search may return:
A. Always the last occurrence
B. Any matching occurrence, depending on implementation
C. Always the first occurrence
D. No occurrence ever
Correct answer: B. Any matching occurrence, depending on implementation
Explanation: Standard binary search does not guarantee first/last duplicate unless modified.
13. To find the first occurrence of a duplicate in a sorted array, binary search can be modified to:
A. Stop at the first match in every case
B. Search only the right half after a match
C. Continue searching left after finding a match
D. Shuffle the array
Correct answer: C. Continue searching left after finding a match
Explanation: The algorithm records the match and keeps looking to its left.
14. To find the last occurrence of a duplicate, binary search can be modified to:
A. Delete duplicate values first
B. Always stop immediately
C. Continue searching right after finding a match
D. Search only left after a match
Correct answer: C. Continue searching right after finding a match
Explanation: The algorithm records the match and keeps looking to its right.
15. In a sorted array, a lower-bound search finds the first position whose value is:
A. Not less than the target
B. Always equal to the largest value
C. Randomly selected
D. Strictly less than the target
Correct answer: A. Not less than the target
Explanation: Lower bound is the first index with value greater than or equal to the target.
16. An upper-bound search commonly finds the first position whose value is:
A. Always the first array index
B. Greater than the target
C. Equal to the array length only
D. Less than or equal to the target
Correct answer: B. Greater than the target
Explanation: Upper bound is the first index with a value strictly greater than the target.
17. A sentinel in linear search is used mainly to:
A. Guarantee O(log n)
B. Sort the array
C. Reduce the need for a separate end check inside the loop
D. Create a binary tree
Correct answer: C. Reduce the need for a separate end check inside the loop
Explanation: A sentinel value can simplify loop checks, though setup and boundary handling remain important.
18. Which method works without requiring sorted input?
A. Linear search
B. Lower-bound search
C. Binary search
D. Binary search tree inorder lookup only
Correct answer: A. Linear search
Explanation: Linear search can scan any sequence regardless of order.
19. Which method is generally faster for a large sorted array?
A. Queue traversal
B. Binary search
C. Bubble search
D. Linear search in all cases
Correct answer: B. Binary search
Explanation: Binary search is logarithmic on sorted random-access data.
20. Why is linear search natural for a linked list?
A. The list is always sorted
B. Nodes are reached by following links sequentially
C. A hash table is built automatically
D. Every node has a direct integer index
Correct answer: B. Nodes are reached by following links sequentially
Explanation: Linked lists typically lack efficient random access to a middle node.
21. A successful search means:
A. The array has been sorted
B. The target is absent
C. The target is found
D. The memory is full
Correct answer: C. The target is found
Explanation: Successful search returns a matching location or value.
22. An unsuccessful search means:
A. The first element always matches
B. The data must be a tree
C. No matching target is found
D. The algorithm cannot terminate
Correct answer: C. No matching target is found
Explanation: A miss occurs when the target is not present in the searched collection.
23. For n elements, linear search may make up to how many element comparisons?
A. 1
B. n
C. n²
D. log₂ n exactly
Correct answer: B. n
Explanation: If the target is last or absent, each of the n elements may be compared.
24. For low = 0 and high = 6, using floor midpoint, mid is:
A. 3
B. 2
C. 6
D. 4
Correct answer: A. 3
Explanation: The midpoint is floor((0+6)/2) = 3.
25. Sorted array [2, 5, 8, 12, 16], target 12: first middle value is:
A. 5
B. 8
C. 2
D. 16
Correct answer: B. 8
Explanation: With low=0 and high=4, mid=floor(4/2)=2 and the value is 8.
26. In [2, 5, 8, 12, 16], after comparing target 12 with middle value 8, next range is:
A. The left portion containing 2 and 5
B. The entire array again
C. The right portion containing 12 and 16
D. An empty range immediately
Correct answer: C. The right portion containing 12 and 16
Explanation: Since 12 is greater than 8, the left half can be discarded.
27. For sorted [3, 7, 9, 14, 20], target 3, the first midpoint value is:
A. 3
B. 20
C. 7
D. 9
Correct answer: D. 9
Explanation: The middle index is 2, containing 9.
28. In a typical binary search, low > high indicates:
A. The algorithm should double the array
B. The search interval is empty
C. The target was found at low
D. The array must be reversed
Correct answer: B. The search interval is empty
Explanation: When the lower bound passes the upper bound, no candidate positions remain.
29. If low = high in binary search, the interval contains:
A. The entire array
B. No candidate elements
C. One candidate element
D. Exactly two elements
Correct answer: C. One candidate element
Explanation: Equal boundaries represent a one-element interval.
30. Why does binary search fit arrays especially well?
A. Array data is always hashed
B. Arrays always use linked pointers
C. Array middle elements can be accessed directly
D. Arrays never contain duplicates
Correct answer: C. Array middle elements can be accessed directly
Explanation: Random access makes midpoint retrieval efficient.
31. Binary search on a basic linked list may lose efficiency because:
A. Linked lists cannot be sorted
B. Finding each midpoint can require traversing nodes
C. A linked list has no data
D. It always takes constant time
Correct answer: B. Finding each midpoint can require traversing nodes
Explanation: Binary search's logarithmic comparison count does not help if midpoint access is linear.
32. Average-case lookup in a well-designed hash table is often:
A. Always O(log n)
B. O(1)
C. O(n²)
D. O(2ⁿ)
Correct answer: B. O(1)
Explanation: Hashing often gives constant expected lookup, though worst cases can be linear.
33. Searching a balanced binary search tree takes:
A. Always O(1)
B. Always O(n²)
C. O(log n) on average/typically when balanced
D. O(2ⁿ)
Correct answer: C. O(log n) on average/typically when balanced
Explanation: A balanced BST has logarithmic height.
34. A search key is:
A. A pointer to the CPU
B. The last instruction in a program
C. A sorting pass
D. The value or field used to locate a record
Correct answer: D. The value or field used to locate a record
Explanation: The key is the attribute compared with stored records during lookup.
35. When using a sentinel, the implementation must ensure:
A. The sentinel setup does not corrupt valid data or boundaries
B. The target is always present
C. All elements are unique
D. The array is converted to a graph
Correct answer: A. The sentinel setup does not corrupt valid data or boundaries
Explanation: Sentinel techniques need careful boundary and data handling.
36. Interpolation search estimates a position using:
A. A random tree rotation
B. The number of queue items
C. Only a stack top
D. The target's value relative to endpoint values
Correct answer: D. The target's value relative to endpoint values
Explanation: It estimates where a key may lie based on value distribution.
37. Interpolation search tends to work best when sorted values are:
A. Roughly uniformly distributed
B. In reverse random order
C. All stored in a linked list
D. Always identical
Correct answer: A. Roughly uniformly distributed
Explanation: Uniform distributions make its position estimates more effective.
38. Jump search typically moves through a sorted array in:
A. Fixed-size jumps, then linearly scans a block
B. Only recursive tree rotations
C. Random jumps forever
D. A full sort after each comparison
Correct answer: A. Fixed-size jumps, then linearly scans a block
Explanation: Jump search skips blocks and then checks within the likely block.
39. Exponential search first:
A. Doubles a bound to find a range, then uses binary search
B. Creates a hash collision
C. Checks only the first element
D. Sorts the data with bubble sort
Correct answer: A. Doubles a bound to find a range, then uses binary search
Explanation: It expands the search range exponentially before binary searching it.
40. Which is the correct typical worst-case comparison?
A. Linear search O(n); binary search O(log n) on sorted random-access data
B. Both always O(1)
C. Linear O(log n); binary O(n²)
D. Both always O(n²)
Correct answer: A. Linear search O(n); binary search O(log n) on sorted random-access data
Explanation: The key advantage of binary search is repeatedly halving a sorted random-access range.
41. If an array changes after sorting, binary search remains valid only if:
A. The array uses strings
B. All values are positive
C. The array length is even
D. The ordering required by the search is preserved
Correct answer: D. The ordering required by the search is preserved
Explanation: Binary search depends on the searched range remaining ordered by the comparison key.
42. A search function may return an index or:
A. A guaranteed sorted array
B. A special not-found value/indicator
C. A graph cycle only
D. A new CPU
Correct answer: B. A special not-found value/indicator
Explanation: Implementations commonly return an index or a designated result when no match exists.
43. For string search, case sensitivity depends on:
A. The graph's degree
B. Whether the stack is empty
C. The array size only
D. The comparison rules used by the implementation
Correct answer: D. The comparison rules used by the implementation
Explanation: A case-sensitive comparison treats uppercase and lowercase letters as different.
44. If a target appears several times, finding all occurrences may require:
A. Stopping after any one match in all implementations
B. Deleting the target
C. Using only a stack
D. Continuing the search beyond the first match
Correct answer: D. Continuing the search beyond the first match
Explanation: To report every match, the algorithm must continue or use a method designed for duplicates.
45. A correct search algorithm should report not found when:
A. The target is at index zero
B. The array is sorted
C. No element matches the target
D. The target appears once
Correct answer: C. No element matches the target
Explanation: The result must accurately reflect whether a matching key exists.
46. Why might (low + high) / 2 be avoided in some languages?
A. Division cannot be used in algorithms
B. low + high can overflow a fixed-width integer
C. It makes the array unsorted
D. It always gives the last index
Correct answer: B. low + high can overflow a fixed-width integer
Explanation: The alternative low + (high-low)/2 avoids the potentially overflowing sum.
47. Sorting data before many searches may be worthwhile when:
A. There is only one tiny search and order must be preserved
B. Searches are forbidden
C. The data cannot be compared
D. The one-time sorting cost is offset by repeated faster searches
Correct answer: D. The one-time sorting cost is offset by repeated faster searches
Explanation: Preprocessing can pay off when many queries reuse the sorted collection.
48. For a small unsorted list, a practical simple choice is often:
A. Heap sort
B. Dijkstra's algorithm
C. Linear search
D. Binary search without sorting
Correct answer: C. Linear search
Explanation: Linear search is simple and works directly without a sorting step.
49. Which statement about linear search is correct?
A. Halving the search range each time
B. Building a tree first
C. Using a hash function only
D. Checking elements one by one
Correct answer: D. Checking elements one by one
Explanation: Linear search examines items sequentially until a match or the end.
50. What is the main idea of linear search complexity?
A. O(1)
B. O(n log n)
C. O(n)
D. O(log n)
Correct answer: C. O(n)
Explanation: The target may be last or absent, requiring all n items to be checked.


5. Sorting Algorithms
Choose the best answer. The correct option and a brief explanation follow each question.
1. Sorting means arranging items according to:
A. A specified order or key
B. Random order
C. Their insertion time in every case
D. Their memory addresses only
Correct answer: A. A specified order or key
Explanation: Sorting orders records by a chosen field, such as ascending numeric value.
2. Bubble sort repeatedly compares:
A. Adjacent elements
B. Tree parents only
C. Only the first and last elements
D. Random graph vertices
Correct answer: A. Adjacent elements
Explanation: Bubble sort swaps adjacent out-of-order elements.
3. Bubble sort's typical worst-case time is:
A. O(n²)
B. O(1)
C. O(n log n)
D. O(log n)
Correct answer: A. O(n²)
Explanation: Nested passes and adjacent comparisons give quadratic worst-case work.
4. With an early-stop flag, optimized bubble sort can be O(n) when:
A. The array is empty only
B. Every key is unique but random
C. The input is reversed
D. The input is already sorted
Correct answer: D. The input is already sorted
Explanation: If a pass makes no swaps, the algorithm can stop after a linear pass.
5. Selection sort repeatedly selects:
A. The newest inserted item
B. The middle element only
C. A random pivot always
D. The minimum (for ascending order) from the unsorted portion
Correct answer: D. The minimum (for ascending order) from the unsorted portion
Explanation: Selection sort places the next smallest element into its final position.
6. Selection sort typically performs at most about how many swaps?
A. n² swaps exactly
B. log₂ n swaps
C. n - 1
D. 2ⁿ swaps
Correct answer: C. n - 1
Explanation: Each pass places one selected element, so at most n−1 swaps are needed.
7. Insertion sort builds a sorted portion by:
A. Hashing every key
B. Splitting a graph into components
C. Choosing a heap root only
D. Inserting each new element into its proper position
Correct answer: D. Inserting each new element into its proper position
Explanation: Each element is inserted into the already-sorted prefix.
8. Insertion sort performs well when input is:
A. A queue with no values
B. A graph
C. Already or nearly sorted
D. Very large and reverse sorted in every case
Correct answer: C. Already or nearly sorted
Explanation: Few shifts are needed when each new item is already near its correct position.
9. Merge sort follows which approach?
A. Divide and conquer
B. Greedy hashing
C. Only adjacent swapping
D. Linear probing
Correct answer: A. Divide and conquer
Explanation: It splits the sequence, sorts subparts, then merges them.
10. Merge sort has typical worst-case time:
A. O(1)
B. O(2ⁿ)
C. O(n²)
D. O(n log n)
Correct answer: D. O(n log n)
Explanation: There are logarithmically many levels, with linear merging per level.
11. A common array implementation of merge sort needs:
A. No memory at all
B. O(n) auxiliary space
C. O(1) space in every implementation
D. O(2ⁿ) space
Correct answer: B. O(n) auxiliary space
Explanation: Merging usually uses a temporary array proportional to the input size.
12. Merge sort can be stable when:
A. All equal keys are deleted
B. It uses a hash table
C. Equal keys from the left run are taken first during merging
D. The input is reversed first
Correct answer: C. Equal keys from the left run are taken first during merging
Explanation: Choosing the left item on equal keys preserves their relative order.
13. Quicksort partitions data around a:
A. Pivot
B. Queue front
C. Hash bucket count
D. Tree root only
Correct answer: A. Pivot
Explanation: Partitioning places elements on sides according to their relation to a pivot.
14. Quicksort's worst-case time can be:
A. O(n²)
B. O(log n)
C. O(1)
D. O(n) in every case
Correct answer: A. O(n²)
Explanation: Highly unbalanced partitions can create quadratic work.
15. Quicksort's average expected time is commonly:
A. O(n²) always
B. O(1)
C. O(2ⁿ)
D. O(n log n)
Correct answer: D. O(n log n)
Explanation: Reasonably balanced partitions yield n log n expected work.
16. Choosing a good pivot helps quicksort by:
A. Making all values equal
B. Keeping partitions reasonably balanced
C. Guaranteeing no comparisons
D. Removing the need for partitioning
Correct answer: B. Keeping partitions reasonably balanced
Explanation: Balanced partitions reduce recursion depth and total work.
17. Heap sort uses a:
A. Heap data structure
B. Queue only
C. Hash collision chain only
D. Trie only
Correct answer: A. Heap data structure
Explanation: Heap sort builds a heap and repeatedly extracts the root.
18. Heap sort's worst-case time is:
A. O(2ⁿ)
B. O(1)
C. O(n²)
D. O(n log n)
Correct answer: D. O(n log n)
Explanation: Heap construction is linear and repeated removals cost logarithmic time.
19. Standard heap sort is generally:
A. Stable only on linked lists
B. Always stable
C. Only stable for strings
D. Not stable
Correct answer: D. Not stable
Explanation: Heap operations can move equal-key elements past each other.
20. Counting sort is most suitable when keys are:
A. Only graph edges
B. Arbitrary complex objects with no key
C. All unbounded real values
D. Integers in a reasonably small known range
Correct answer: D. Integers in a reasonably small known range
Explanation: Counting sort counts occurrences of each key value rather than comparing pairs.
21. Counting sort can run in O(n + k), where k is:
A. The key range size
B. Always the number of arrays
C. The number of recursive calls only
D. The CPU clock rate
Correct answer: A. The key range size
Explanation: Its work depends on both item count and the range of possible keys.
22. Radix sort processes keys by:
A. Following tree parent links
B. Digits or character positions
C. Comparing all pairs
D. Repeatedly choosing a pivot only
Correct answer: B. Digits or character positions
Explanation: Radix sort sorts by successive digit/character positions.
23. Radix sort commonly relies on each digit-level sort being:
A. Quadratic in all cases
B. Stable
C. Randomized
D. A graph traversal
Correct answer: B. Stable
Explanation: Stability preserves earlier digit ordering while sorting later positions.
24. Bucket sort distributes items into:
A. Buckets, then sorts or processes each bucket
B. A single stack only
C. CPU registers by name
D. Tree leaves only
Correct answer: A. Buckets, then sorts or processes each bucket
Explanation: Bucket sort works well when values distribute suitably across buckets.
25. Comparison-based sorting has a general worst-case lower bound of:
A. Ω(n²) for all algorithms
B. Ω(1) for all inputs
C. Ω(2ⁿ)
D. Ω(n log n)
Correct answer: D. Ω(n log n)
Explanation: For general comparison sorting, decision-tree arguments give an n log n lower bound.
26. Which sorting algorithm is stable in its standard common form?
A. Quicksort
B. Heap sort
C. Merge sort
D. Selection sort
Correct answer: C. Merge sort
Explanation: Merge sort can preserve the relative order of equal-key records.
27. Which is commonly in-place in its standard array implementation?
A. External merge sort
B. Merge sort with an auxiliary array
C. Counting sort in its usual form
D. Selection sort
Correct answer: D. Selection sort
Explanation: Selection sort uses constant auxiliary storage aside from the input array.
28. An adaptive sorting algorithm benefits from:
A. All values being stored in a graph
B. Using only negative numbers
C. Having no input
D. Existing order in the input
Correct answer: D. Existing order in the input
Explanation: Adaptive methods do less work when the data already has useful order.
29. External sorting is useful when:
A. No storage is available
B. Data must remain unsorted
C. Data does not fit in main memory
D. Only two values exist
Correct answer: C. Data does not fit in main memory
Explanation: External algorithms process data using secondary storage, often merging sorted runs.
30. Ascending numeric order means:
A. Insertion order only
B. Smallest to largest
C. Random order
D. Largest to smallest
Correct answer: B. Smallest to largest
Explanation: Ascending order increases from lower to higher values.
31. Descending numeric order means:
A. Random order
B. Smallest to largest
C. Alphabetical only
D. Largest to smallest
Correct answer: D. Largest to smallest
Explanation: Descending order decreases from higher to lower values.
32. In a standard bubble-sort pass, the largest unsorted value tends to move:
A. To the root of a tree
B. Into a hash bucket
C. Toward the start always
D. Toward the end
Correct answer: D. Toward the end
Explanation: Repeated adjacent swaps push a large value rightward in an ascending pass.
33. After one ascending selection-sort pass, the first position contains:
A. A random item
B. The median in every case
C. The largest element always
D. The smallest element from the unsorted input
Correct answer: D. The smallest element from the unsorted input
Explanation: Selection sort places the minimum remaining key at the current front position.
34. During insertion sort, the processed prefix is:
A. Always empty
B. A graph
C. Always reversed
D. Sorted
Correct answer: D. Sorted
Explanation: The invariant is that the portion already processed remains sorted.
35. Merging two sorted lists takes O(n) time in total because:
A. Every pair must be compared
B. Each item is compared/copied a bounded number of times
C. It uses exponential recursion
D. The lists must be hashed
Correct answer: B. Each item is compared/copied a bounded number of times
Explanation: A merge advances through the two runs without repeatedly revisiting items.
36. Quicksort partitioning aims to:
A. Build an adjacency matrix
B. Fully sort every partition immediately
C. Place items on appropriate sides of the pivot
D. Count only duplicate values
Correct answer: C. Place items on appropriate sides of the pivot
Explanation: Partitioning separates smaller and larger elements according to the pivot rule.
37. Which algorithm is often a good choice for small or nearly sorted arrays?
A. Dijkstra
B. Counting sort for arbitrary strings
C. Insertion sort
D. Worst-case quicksort with bad pivot
Correct answer: C. Insertion sort
Explanation: Insertion sort has low overhead and near-linear behavior on nearly sorted data.
38. Which is a reliable O(n log n) worst-case comparison sort?
A. Merge sort
B. Insertion sort
C. Selection sort
D. Bubble sort
Correct answer: A. Merge sort
Explanation: Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) worst-case time.
39. Sorting records by student ID means the student ID is the:
A. Stack pointer
B. Hash collision
C. Sort key
D. Tree height
Correct answer: C. Sort key
Explanation: The sort key is the field used to determine record order.
40. Stable sorting is useful for multi-key sorting because it:
A. Makes every key unique
B. Removes all equal records
C. Avoids all comparisons
D. Preserves earlier ordering among equal values of the current key
Correct answer: D. Preserves earlier ordering among equal values of the current key
Explanation: A stable second sort can preserve the ordering established by a previous sort.
41. A comparison sort determines order mainly by:
A. Counting only digits without comparisons
B. Following a fixed graph route
C. Comparing keys
D. Using CPU temperature
Correct answer: C. Comparing keys
Explanation: Comparison sorts use pairwise key comparisons to order elements.
42. A sorted result should contain:
A. Half the input values
B. New random values
C. Only unique elements
D. The same elements as the input, arranged in the required order
Correct answer: D. The same elements as the input, arranged in the required order
Explanation: A correct sort changes order, not the multiset of items.
43. If two records have equal keys, a stable sort keeps them:
A. In their original relative order
B. At random positions
C. Removed from output
D. Always reversed
Correct answer: A. In their original relative order
Explanation: Stability preserves the relative order of equal-key records.
44. Which sort commonly needs extra memory for merging arrays?
A. Merge sort
B. In-place quicksort in typical implementations
C. Selection sort
D. In-place heapsort
Correct answer: A. Merge sort
Explanation: Array merge sort normally allocates temporary storage for combining runs.
45. Quicksort's auxiliary stack space depends mainly on:
A. Only the largest key
B. Partition balance and recursion depth
C. The number of buckets in a hash table
D. The graph's edge weights
Correct answer: B. Partition balance and recursion depth
Explanation: Balanced recursion uses logarithmic stack depth; poor partitions can deepen it.
46. For a very small array, a simple quadratic sort can be reasonable because:
A. It never compares values
B. It becomes O(log n)
C. It uses no instructions
D. Its overhead is low and the input is small
Correct answer: D. Its overhead is low and the input is small
Explanation: Asymptotic complexity is not the only factor; constants and input size matter.
47. Why can counting sort be inefficient for a huge key range?
A. The counting array may require excessive memory
B. It must compare every pair
C. It always uses recursion
D. It cannot sort integers
Correct answer: A. The counting array may require excessive memory
Explanation: Its space and time depend on the size of the key range.
48. Radix sort is most naturally applied when keys can be:
A. Never represented as symbols
B. Compared only by pointer address
C. Examined digit/character position by position
D. Stored only in a tree
Correct answer: C. Examined digit/character position by position
Explanation: Radix sorting assumes a suitable positional representation and stable digit-level sorting.
49. A fair sorting benchmark should use:
A. Different hardware for each algorithm without noting it
B. Only one favorable case
C. Representative inputs and consistent measurement conditions
D. Only the algorithm names
Correct answer: C. Representative inputs and consistent measurement conditions
Explanation: Input size, distribution, environment, and measurement method affect results.
50. Sorting before searching is often helpful when:
A. The original order must never change and no copy is allowed
B. There is no way to compare keys
C. Many searches will be performed on the same data
D. The data is constantly changing after every query
Correct answer: C. Many searches will be performed on the same data
Explanation: A one-time sort may be worthwhile when repeated binary searches follow.


6. Hashing
Choose the best answer. The correct option and a brief explanation follow each question.
1. Hashing maps a key to:
A. A sorted list automatically
B. A queue position based only on arrival
C. A tree height only
D. A table index or bucket using a hash function
Correct answer: D. A table index or bucket using a hash function
Explanation: A hash function transforms a key into an index used for storage or lookup.
2. A hash function should ideally:
A. Return only negative values
B. Map every key to one slot
C. Distribute keys evenly across the table
D. Require keys to be sorted
Correct answer: C. Distribute keys evenly across the table
Explanation: Good distribution reduces collisions and improves expected performance.
3. A hash table stores data using:
A. Only tree leaves
B. Hash-derived positions or buckets
C. Only a linked list with no keys
D. Only sequential scanning
Correct answer: B. Hash-derived positions or buckets
Explanation: Hash tables use hash values to locate entries quickly.
4. A hash collision occurs when:
A. Different keys map to the same table position
B. A sorting pass ends
C. A table has no empty slot
D. Two keys are necessarily identical
Correct answer: A. Different keys map to the same table position
Explanation: Collisions are unavoidable when the key space exceeds the number of slots.
5. Separate chaining handles collisions by:
A. Reversing the table
B. Moving every item to a tree root
C. Deleting the new key always
D. Keeping multiple entries in a bucket, often in a linked list
Correct answer: D. Keeping multiple entries in a bucket, often in a linked list
Explanation: Each bucket can contain a collection of entries with the same hash index.
6. Open addressing resolves collisions by:
A. Using recursion only
B. Storing all items only outside the table
C. Probing for another slot in the table
D. Building a graph
Correct answer: C. Probing for another slot in the table
Explanation: The probe sequence searches alternative table positions.
7. Linear probing checks:
A. Only the first bucket
B. A tree's left subtree
C. Only random nodes
D. Consecutive table slots until a suitable one is found
Correct answer: D. Consecutive table slots until a suitable one is found
Explanation: Linear probing moves through slots one at a time, wrapping around if needed.
8. Quadratic probing changes probe positions using:
A. Only the next consecutive slot
B. A binary search tree traversal
C. Quadratic offsets
D. The queue front
Correct answer: C. Quadratic offsets
Explanation: Quadratic offsets reduce some clustering patterns compared with linear probing.
9. Double hashing uses:
A. Two roots in a tree
B. A queue and a stack together
C. A second hash function to determine probe steps
D. Two sorted arrays only
Correct answer: C. A second hash function to determine probe steps
Explanation: A second hash function helps define the probing sequence.
10. Hash-table load factor is commonly:
A. Number of stored entries divided by table capacity
B. Table capacity divided by CPU speed
C. Number of collisions squared
D. Number of keys times table height
Correct answer: A. Number of stored entries divided by table capacity
Explanation: Load factor measures how full a table is.
11. A high load factor in open addressing generally leads to:
A. More probes on average
B. A smaller table automatically
C. Guaranteed O(1) worst case
D. No collisions ever
Correct answer: A. More probes on average
Explanation: As slots fill, finding an empty slot or a key usually requires more probing.
12. Rehashing usually means:
A. Sorting every key alphabetically only
B. Deleting the hash function
C. Converting the table into a queue
D. Building a larger/new table and reinserting entries
Correct answer: D. Building a larger/new table and reinserting entries
Explanation: Changing capacity changes key positions, so entries are inserted again using the hash function.
13. Expected lookup time in a well-designed hash table is often:
A. O(2ⁿ)
B. O(n²)
C. O(1)
D. Always O(log n)
Correct answer: C. O(1)
Explanation: With good distribution and controlled load factor, average lookup is constant time.
14. Worst-case lookup in a hash table can be:
A. O(1/n)
B. Always O(1)
C. O(n)
D. Always O(log n)
Correct answer: C. O(n)
Explanation: Severe collisions can force a scan through many entries.
15. If two keys are equal under the table's key equality rule, they should:
A. Never be stored
B. Always produce different hash values
C. Be placed in separate tables
D. Produce the same hash value
Correct answer: D. Produce the same hash value
Explanation: A fundamental hash-table requirement is that equal keys have equal hashes.
16. If two keys have the same hash value, they are:
A. Impossible to store
B. Always equal
C. Not necessarily equal
D. Always strings
Correct answer: C. Not necessarily equal
Explanation: Different keys can map to the same hash value; this is a collision.
17. The division method commonly computes a hash index using:
A. The key's tree depth
B. key divided by CPU frequency
C. key mod table size
D. key multiplied by table size only
Correct answer: C. key mod table size
Explanation: Modulo maps an integer key into a range of table indices.
18. Why can table size affect hashing performance?
A. It removes the need for a hash function
B. It affects index distribution and collision frequency
C. It makes all lookups linear
D. It changes every key's meaning
Correct answer: B. It affects index distribution and collision frequency
Explanation: Capacity and its choice can influence distribution and load factor.
19. Primary clustering is especially associated with:
A. Linear probing
B. Separate chaining only
C. Binary search
D. Merge sort
Correct answer: A. Linear probing
Explanation: Consecutive occupied runs can grow with linear probing and attract more keys.
20. Deleting from an open-addressed table often needs a special marker because:
A. The hash function cannot read keys
B. Every deleted key must be sorted
C. All keys are duplicated
D. A truly empty slot could incorrectly stop a later search
Correct answer: D. A truly empty slot could incorrectly stop a later search
Explanation: A tombstone preserves the probe chain so searches can continue.
21. A tombstone marks a slot as:
A. A table's root
B. A sorted key
C. Never allocated and always a stopping point
D. Previously occupied but deleted
Correct answer: D. Previously occupied but deleted
Explanation: Tombstones distinguish deleted slots from slots that were never used.
22. In separate chaining, deleting an entry usually involves:
A. Shifting every table entry
B. Changing every hash value
C. Rebuilding the whole table always
D. Removing it from its bucket's collection
Correct answer: D. Removing it from its bucket's collection
Explanation: Only the relevant bucket structure usually needs updating.
23. A hash key should ideally be:
A. Always the same for every record
B. Stable while the entry is stored
C. Changed on every lookup
D. Based on random time every time
Correct answer: B. Stable while the entry is stored
Explanation: If a key's hash-relevant state changes, lookup may no longer find its entry.
24. A map/dictionary commonly uses hashing to support:
A. Only graph traversal
B. Only sorting by position
C. Only stack pop
D. Key-value lookup
Correct answer: D. Key-value lookup
Explanation: Hash maps associate keys with values and use the key to locate an entry.
25. A hash set is commonly used to maintain:
A. A collection of unique keys/items
B. A CPU process queue
C. A sorted tree in every implementation
D. A sequence with required duplicates
Correct answer: A. A collection of unique keys/items
Explanation: Sets represent membership and avoid duplicate elements according to equality rules.
26. A hash set is useful for a fast:
A. Array insertion at index zero
B. Membership test
C. Stable merge
D. Level-order traversal
Correct answer: B. Membership test
Explanation: A membership query checks whether an item is present.
27. A cryptographic hash function is designed for properties such as:
A. Sorting records
B. Always returning the original key
C. Guaranteed reversible encryption
D. Preimage resistance and collision resistance
Correct answer: D. Preimage resistance and collision resistance
Explanation: Cryptographic hashes have security goals beyond ordinary table-index distribution.
28. A hash function differs from encryption because hashing is generally:
A. One-way rather than designed to be decrypted
B. A sorting algorithm
C. Always reversible with a secret key
D. A queue operation
Correct answer: A. One-way rather than designed to be decrypted
Explanation: Encryption is designed to be reversible with the appropriate key; hashing normally is not.
29. For password storage, systems should use:
A. The same fixed hash for every user
B. Plain unsalted fast hash only
C. A password-hashing scheme with salt and a suitable work factor
D. Reversible encoding
Correct answer: C. A password-hashing scheme with salt and a suitable work factor
Explanation: Password hashing should make large-scale guessing costly and use a unique salt.
30. In password hashing, a salt is:
A. The user's password shown in plain text
B. A collision-resolution probe
C. The hash-table capacity
D. A random value stored with the password hash
Correct answer: D. A random value stored with the password hash
Explanation: A salt helps prevent precomputed attacks and identical passwords producing identical stored hashes.
31. A uniform hash distribution means keys are:
A. Spread roughly evenly among table positions
B. All placed in one bucket
C. Always stored alphabetically
D. Never compared
Correct answer: A. Spread roughly evenly among table positions
Explanation: Even distribution helps reduce collision concentration.
32. A perfect hash function for a fixed key set has:
A. A collision for every key
B. No collisions among those keys
C. Only one possible key
D. No output index
Correct answer: B. No collisions among those keys
Explanation: Perfect hashing maps a specified set of keys to distinct slots.
33. A table may resize when:
A. Its load factor crosses a chosen threshold
B. The table has no hash function
C. A search misses exactly once in all designs
D. A key is read once
Correct answer: A. Its load factor crosses a chosen threshold
Explanation: Implementations often resize to keep performance acceptable as entries change.
34. A hash index for a table of capacity m should normally be in:
A. 0 through m - 1 for zero-based indexing
B. Only m
C. Any negative integer
D. 1 through m only
Correct answer: A. 0 through m - 1 for zero-based indexing
Explanation: The computed index must refer to a valid slot.
35. Using h(k)=k mod 10, the hash index for key 37 is:
A. 3
B. 7
C. 37
D. 10
Correct answer: B. 7
Explanation: 37 modulo 10 leaves remainder 7.
36. Using h(k)=k mod 10, keys 12 and 22:
A. Map to indices 1 and 2
B. Always occupy index 12 and 22
C. Cannot be hashed
D. Collide at index 2
Correct answer: D. Collide at index 2
Explanation: Both 12 mod 10 and 22 mod 10 equal 2.
37. With separate chaining, lookup time depends partly on:
A. Only the color of the table
B. The array's sorting stability
C. The number of tree roots
D. The length of the selected bucket's chain
Correct answer: D. The length of the selected bucket's chain
Explanation: A long chain increases the number of comparisons needed in that bucket.
38. In open addressing, the table must generally have:
A. An available slot for inserting a new distinct entry
B. Only one bucket
C. No empty slots before any insertion
D. A separate linked list for every key
Correct answer: A. An available slot for inserting a new distinct entry
Explanation: Insertion needs a slot reachable by its probing sequence.
39. A poor hash function often causes:
A. All keys to become equal
B. The table to sort itself
C. Guaranteed faster lookups
D. Many collisions and slower operations
Correct answer: D. Many collisions and slower operations
Explanation: Uneven distribution concentrates entries and increases work.
40. A hash table generally does not guarantee:
A. Collision handling
B. Key-based lookup
C. Storing key-value pairs
D. Items returned in sorted key order
Correct answer: D. Items returned in sorted key order
Explanation: Hash placement is not designed to preserve sorted order.
41. Compared with a balanced BST, a hash table is often better for:
A. Inorder traversal
B. Range queries in sorted order
C. Finding predecessor/successor by order
D. Expected exact-key lookup when sorted order is unnecessary
Correct answer: D. Expected exact-key lookup when sorted order is unnecessary
Explanation: Hash tables offer expected constant-time exact lookup but do not naturally maintain order.
42. Why is a balanced BST often better than a hash table for range queries?
A. Hash tables cannot store numbers
B. It never compares keys
C. It has no pointers
D. It maintains keys in sorted order
Correct answer: D. It maintains keys in sorted order
Explanation: Ordered trees can efficiently locate a range and traverse its keys in order.
43. In a typical map, inserting an existing key may:
A. Replace or update the value associated with that key
B. Always create a second identical key entry
C. Delete the entire table
D. Force the key to be sorted
Correct answer: A. Replace or update the value associated with that key
Explanation: Map behavior usually treats keys as unique, with repeated insertion updating the value.
44. Why are collisions unavoidable for many hash tables?
A. Hash functions cannot return numbers
B. There are more possible keys than table slots
C. All keys are identical
D. The table has infinite capacity
Correct answer: B. There are more possible keys than table slots
Explanation: By the pigeonhole principle, a finite table cannot assign every possible key a unique slot.
45. The pigeonhole principle implies that if more distinct keys than slots are mapped, then:
A. Every key gets a unique slot
B. The table must be sorted
C. At least two keys share a slot
D. No hash value is returned
Correct answer: C. At least two keys share a slot
Explanation: More items than slots guarantees at least one shared slot.
46. Rehashing can take O(n) or more work because:
A. It sorts all possible keys
B. Stored entries must be placed into the new table
C. It never examines entries
D. It only changes a title
Correct answer: B. Stored entries must be placed into the new table
Explanation: Moving n stored entries requires processing those entries; exact cost depends on implementation.
47. For a stored key, a deterministic hash function should return:
A. A value outside all table bounds
B. A new random value on each call
C. The same hash value while the key and hashing rules remain unchanged
D. Only zero
Correct answer: C. The same hash value while the key and hashing rules remain unchanged
Explanation: Consistent hashes are necessary to locate previously stored entries.
48. Which pair are common collision-resolution methods?
A. Separate chaining and open addressing
B. Merge sort and quicksort
C. Push and pop
D. BFS and DFS
Correct answer: A. Separate chaining and open addressing
Explanation: Chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket collection; open addressing probes other slots.
49. Which is a common use of hashing?
A. Only arranging numbers in ascending order
B. Only traversing a tree by level
C. Only allocating CPU time
D. Fast lookup in dictionaries and caches
Correct answer: D. Fast lookup in dictionaries and caches
Explanation: Hashing is widely used for maps, sets, caches, and indexing.
50. Which statement about hashing is correct?
A. A table index or bucket using a hash function
B. A sorted list automatically
C. A tree height only
D. A queue position based only on arrival
Correct answer: A. A table index or bucket using a hash function
Explanation: A hash function transforms a key into an index used for storage or lookup.

7. Tree Algorithms
Q1. Preorder traversal visits nodes in which order?
A. Root, left subtree, right subtree
B. Left, right, root
C. Left, root, right
D. Level by level only
Correct option: A. Root, left subtree, right subtree
Q2. Which statement is most accurate? Preorder traversal visits nodes in which order?
A. Root, left subtree, right subtree
B. Level by level only
C. Left, root, right
D. Left, right, root
Correct option: A. Root, left subtree, right subtree
Q3. Inorder traversal of a binary tree visits:
A. Root, left, right
B. Right, root, left always
C. Left subtree, root, right subtree
D. Left, right, root
Correct option: C. Left subtree, root, right subtree
Q4. Which statement is most accurate? Inorder traversal of a binary tree visits:
A. Left, right, root
B. Root, left, right
C. Right, root, left always
D. Left subtree, root, right subtree
Correct option: D. Left subtree, root, right subtree
Q5. Postorder traversal visits:
A. Left subtree, right subtree, root
B. Left, root, right
C. Root, left, right
D. Root only
Correct option: A. Left subtree, right subtree, root
Q6. Which statement is most accurate? Postorder traversal visits:
A. Left subtree, right subtree, root
B. Left, root, right
C. Root only
D. Root, left, right
Correct option: A. Left subtree, right subtree, root
Q7. Level-order traversal typically uses a:
A. Recursive call stack only
B. Stack only
C. Queue
D. Hash function only
Correct option: C. Queue
Q8. Which statement is most accurate? Level-order traversal typically uses a:
A. Recursive call stack only
B. Stack only
C. Hash function only
D. Queue
Correct option: D. Queue
Q9. A BST search is O(log n) on average when the tree is:
A. A chain
B. Reasonably balanced
C. Always empty
D. Stored as a queue
Correct option: B. Reasonably balanced
Q10. Which statement is most accurate? A BST search is O(log n) on average when the tree is:
A. Always empty
B. Stored as a queue
C. A chain
D. Reasonably balanced
Correct option: D. Reasonably balanced
Q11. Worst-case search in a skewed BST is:
A. O(n log n)
B. O(log log n)
C. O(n)
D. O(1)
Correct option: C. O(n)
Q12. Which statement is most accurate? Worst-case search in a skewed BST is:
A. O(1)
B. O(n log n)
C. O(n)
D. O(log log n)
Correct option: C. O(n)
Q13. AVL trees maintain balance using:
A. Rotations after insertions/deletions as needed
B. Sorting the whole tree after every search
C. Only a queue
D. Hash collisions
Correct option: A. Rotations after insertions/deletions as needed
Q14. Which statement is most accurate? AVL trees maintain balance using:
A. Rotations after insertions/deletions as needed
B. Only a queue
C. Hash collisions
D. Sorting the whole tree after every search
Correct option: A. Rotations after insertions/deletions as needed
Q15. For an AVL node, the balance factor is commonly:
A. Number of keys times height
B. Root index minus leaf index
C. Number of edges squared
D. Height(left) minus height(right)
Correct option: D. Height(left) minus height(right)
Q16. Which statement is most accurate? For an AVL node, the balance factor is commonly:
A. Number of keys times height
B. Height(left) minus height(right)
C. Number of edges squared
D. Root index minus leaf index
Correct option: B. Height(left) minus height(right)
Q17. A rotation in a self-balancing BST aims to:
A. Restore balance while preserving BST ordering
B. Turn the tree into a graph with cycles
C. Delete all leaves
D. Sort an array directly
Correct option: A. Restore balance while preserving BST ordering
Q18. Which statement is most accurate? A rotation in a self-balancing BST aims to:
A. Sort an array directly
B. Turn the tree into a graph with cycles
C. Delete all leaves
D. Restore balance while preserving BST ordering
Correct option: D. Restore balance while preserving BST ordering
Q19. A min-heap keeps the:
A. Largest key at the root
B. Most recently inserted key at the root
C. Median always at the root
D. Smallest key at the root
Correct option: D. Smallest key at the root
Q20. Which statement is most accurate? A min-heap keeps the:
A. Most recently inserted key at the root
B. Smallest key at the root
C. Largest key at the root
D. Median always at the root
Correct option: B. Smallest key at the root
Q21. In a heap stored in a zero-indexed array, left child of index i is:
A. 2i + 2
B. 2i
C. i/2
D. 2i + 1
Correct option: D. 2i + 1
Q22. Which statement is most accurate? In a heap stored in a zero-indexed array, left child of index i is:
A. 2i
B. 2i + 1
C. 2i + 2
D. i/2
Correct option: B. 2i + 1
Q23. In a zero-indexed heap, right child of index i is:
A. i - 1
B. 2i + 2
C. 2i + 1
D. i/2
Correct option: B. 2i + 2
Q24. Which statement is most accurate? In a zero-indexed heap, right child of index i is:
A. i/2
B. i - 1
C. 2i + 1
D. 2i + 2
Correct option: D. 2i + 2
Q25. Heap insertion restores heap order by:
A. Traversing inorder
B. Always sorting all elements
C. Deleting the root
D. Sifting/bubbling the new item upward
Correct option: D. Sifting/bubbling the new item upward
Q26. Which statement is most accurate? Heap insertion restores heap order by:
A. Always sorting all elements
B. Traversing inorder
C. Deleting the root
D. Sifting/bubbling the new item upward
Correct option: D. Sifting/bubbling the new item upward
Q27. Extracting the maximum from a max-heap usually takes:
A. O(log n)
B. O(1) including reheapification
C. O(2I)
D. O(n²)
Correct option: A. O(log n)
Q28. Which statement is most accurate? Extracting the maximum from a max-heap usually takes:
A. O(n²)
B. O(2I)
C. O(1) including reheapification
D. O(log n)
Correct option: D. O(log n)
Q29. Building a heap from n elements can be done in:
A. O(n²) necessarily
B. O(n)
C. O(log n)
D. O(n log n) only, never O(n)
Correct option: B. O(n)
Q30. Which statement is most accurate? Building a heap from n elements can be done in:
A. O(log n)
B. O(n²) necessarily
C. O(n)
D. O(n log n) only, never O(n)
Correct option: C. O(n)
Q31. A B-tree is designed to work efficiently with:
A. Unsorted strings only
B. Stack recursion only
C. Only two total nodes
D. Disk/block storage and many children per node
Correct option: D. Disk/block storage and many children per node
Q32. Which statement is most accurate? A B-tree is designed to work efficiently with:
A. Only two total nodes
B. Disk/block storage and many children per node
C. Unsorted strings only
D. Stack recursion only
Correct option: B. Disk/block storage and many children per node
Q33. A trie node represents a:
A. Queue front
B. Prefix position in a key/string
C. Heap priority only
D. Graph edge weight only
Correct option: B. Prefix position in a key/string
Q34. Which statement is most accurate? A trie node represents a:
A. Queue front
B. Graph edge weight only
C. Prefix position in a key/string
D. Heap priority only
Correct option: C. Prefix position in a key/string
Q35. Deleting a BST node with two children can replace it with:
A. Only the root
B. Any random node
C. A queue
D. Its inorder successor or predecessor
Correct option: D. Its inorder successor or predecessor
Q36. Which statement is most accurate? Deleting a BST node with two children can replace it with:
A. Its inorder successor or predecessor
B. A queue
C. Any random node
D. Only the root
Correct option: A. Its inorder successor or predecessor
Q37. The height of a tree is commonly the number of edges on the longest:
A. Sibling-to-sibling path
B. Root-to-leaf path
C. Cycle
D. Array index
Correct option: B. Root-to-leaf path
Q38. Which statement is most accurate? The height of a tree is commonly the number of edges on the longest:

Q26. Which statement is most accurate? If T(n)=T(n/2)+O(1), the runtime is:
A. O(n)
B. O(log n)
C. O(1)
D. O(n²)
Correct option: B. O(log n)
Q27. If an algorithm uses a table of n by n entries, its table space is:
A. O(log n)

D. O(n²)
Correct option: D. O(n²)
Q28. Which statement is most accurate? If an algorithm uses a table of n by n entries, its table space is:
A. O(log n)

Correct option: C. O(n²)
Q29. An optimization that changes the algorithm should preserve:
A. Only the output formatting

Correct option: D. Correctness and required behavior

C. Only the output formatting
D. Correctness and required behavior
Correct option: D. Correctness and required behavior
Q31. Premature optimization is discouraged because:
A. Correctness is irrelevant

D. It can add complexity before a real bottleneck is understood
Correct option: D. It can add complexity before a real bottleneck is understood
Q32. Which statement is most accurate? Premature optimization is discouraged because:

B. It can add complexity before a real bottleneck is understood
C. Correctness is irrelevant
D. Programs should never be measured
Correct option: B. It can add complexity before a real bottleneck is understood
Q33. Profiling is used to:
A. Replace testing
B. Sort data

D. Prove every algorithm correct automatically
Correct option: C. Identify where a program spends time/resources
Q34. Which statement is most accurate? Profiling is used to:
A. Replace testing

C. Identify where a program spends time/resources
D. Sort data
Correct option: C. Identify where a program spends time/resources
Q35. A bottleneck is:
A. A component that limits overall performance
B. The smallest variable name
C. A mathematical constant only
D. A queue element
Correct option: A. A component that limits overall performance
Q36. Which statement is most accurate? A bottleneck is:
A. A component that limits overall performance
B. The smallest variable name
C. A mathematical constant only
D. A queue element
Correct option: A. A component that limits overall performance
Q37. Space-time trade-off means:
A. Memory has no effect
B. Extra memory may reduce runtime, or less memory may cost time
C. Both are always constant
D. Space equals time exactly
Correct option: B. Extra memory may reduce runtime, or less memory may cost time
Q38. Which statement is most accurate? Space-time trade-off means:
A. Memory has no effect
B. Both are always constant
C. Space equals time exactly
D. Extra memory may reduce runtime, or less memory may cost time
Correct option: D. Extra memory may reduce runtime, or less memory may cost time
Q39. Cache locality can improve performance because:
A. It makes all data sorted
B. It removes algorithmic complexity
C. Nearby/recent data may be accessed faster by cache
D. Cache always slows execution
Correct option: C. Nearby/recent data may be accessed faster by cache
Q40. Which statement is most accurate? Cache locality can improve performance because:
A. Nearby/recent data may be accessed faster by cache
B. It removes algorithmic complexity
C. It makes all data sorted
D. Cache always slows execution
Correct option: A. Nearby/recent data may be accessed faster by cache
Q41. Worst-case analysis is valuable because:
A. It gives a bound on the maximum work for a given input size
B. It predicts exact seconds on all machines
C. It ignores input size
D. It measures only average behavior
Correct option: A. It gives a bound on the maximum work for a given input size
Q42. Which statement is most accurate? Worst-case analysis is valuable because:

B. It ignores input size
C. It predicts exact seconds on all machines
D. It gives a bound on the maximum work for a given input size
Correct option: D. It gives a bound on the maximum work for a given input size
Q43. Average-case analysis requires:
A. A model/distribution of possible inputs
B. A sorted output
C. No assumptions about inputs
D. Only the worst input
Correct option: A. A model/distribution of possible inputs
Q44. Which statement is most accurate? Average-case analysis requires:

B. No assumptions about inputs
C. A model/distribution of possible inputs
D. Only the worst input
Correct option: C. A model/distribution of possible inputs
Q45. An exponential-time algorithm may become impractical because:
A. Runtime can grow dramatically with each increase in input size
B. It never uses recursion

Correct option: A. Runtime can grow dramatically with each increase in input size
Q46. Which statement is most accurate? An exponential-time algorithm may become impractical because:
A. It never uses recursion
B. Runtime can grow dramatically with each increase in input size
C. Its input must be sorted

Correct option: B. Runtime can grow dramatically with each increase in input size
Q47. Optimization should normally begin after:

Correct option: D. Correctness is established and performance is measured
Q48. Which statement is most accurate? Optimization should normally begin after:
A. Memory is disabled
B. The output is guessed
C. Correctness is established and performance is measured
D. All code is deleted
Correct option: C. Correctness is established and performance is measured
Q49. An algorithm is asymptotically faster than another if:
A. Its growth rate is lower for sufficiently large input sizes

D. It uses more variable names
Correct option: A. Its growth rate is lower for sufficiently large input sizes

B. It uses more variable names
